fuentes/documento-de-hamas-2017/resumen.texto: Document presented in Doha: the conflict is with the “Zionist project” and not with the Jews because of their religion; it accepts a Palestinian state on the 1967 lines as a “formula of national consensus”, without recognizing Israel or renouncing the “liberation of all Palestine” or armed resistance.

fuentes/nuestra-lucha-con-los-judios/res.texto: Essay that presents the Jews as permanent enemies of Islam since the days of Medina and as conspirators behind the ills of the modern world. Saudi Arabia republished and distributed it in 1970.

fuentes/nuestra-lucha-con-los-judios/por.texto: It is a link between the anti-Jewish passages of some classical Islamic texts and the reception of European antisemitism in modern Islamism.

fuentes/hitos/resumen.texto: Written in prison: the world, including Muslim societies, has returned to pre-Islamic ignorance (jahiliyya), and a vanguard must restore the sovereignty of God through preaching and jihad.

fuentes/hitos/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most influential text of radical Islamism; it was read by Egyptian Islamic Jihad, al-Qaeda and many others.

fuentes/defensa-de-las-tierras-musulmana.texto: Fatwa according to which, when an enemy occupies Muslim land, jihad becomes an individual duty of every Muslim, like prayer, without the need for permission from parents or rulers; Afghanistan and Palestine are the foremost cases.
It was the basis for recruiting foreign volunteers in Afghanistan and for the ideas of al-Qaeda.

fuentes/declaracion-de-guerra-de-bin-lad.texto: Declaration of War against the Americans Occupying the Land of the Two Holy Places
Message calling for the expulsion of American troops from Saudi Arabia and denouncing a “Zionist-Crusader alliance” against Muslims, from Palestine to Bosnia.

fuentes/fatua-de-1998/titulo.texto: Fatwa of the World Islamic Front against Jews and Crusaders

fuentes/fatua-de-1998/resumen.texto: Fatwa signed by Bin Laden, Ayman al-Zawahiri and others: killing Americans and their allies, civilian or military, is an individual duty of every Muslim in any country, until the al-Aqsa Mosque and the mosque of Mecca are liberated.

fuentes/fatua-de-1998/por_que_importa.texto: It preceded the bombings of the United States embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (1998) and the 11 September 2001 attacks.

fuentes/nostra-aetate/resumen.texto: Declaration of the Council on non-Christian religions: the Church regards “with esteem” the Muslims, who worship the one God, and urges that past quarrels be forgotten; it rejects the collective guilt of the Jews for the death of Jesus and deplores antisemitism.

fuentes/nostra-aetate/por_que_importa.texto: It changed the Catholic Church's official relationship with Judaism and Islam.

fuentes/conferencia-de-ratisbona-texto/r.texto: Lecture on the relationship between faith and reason that criticizes an idea of God detached from reason —in Islam and in currents of Western theology— and the “dehellenization” of Christianity; it quotes Manuel II's dialogue on violence in religion.

fuentes/una-palabra-comun/titulo.texto: A Common Word Between Us and You

fuentes/una-palabra-comun/resumen.texto: Open letter from Muslim scholars to Christian leaders: love of God and love of neighbour are the common foundation of Islam and Christianity and the basis for peace between them.

fuentes/documento-sobre-la-fraternidad-h.texto: Pope Francis and Grand Imam Ahmed al-Tayeb
Joint declaration that condemns the use of religion to justify violence and terrorism and defends freedom of belief and full citizenship for minorities.

fuentes/orientalismo/resumen.texto: Essay analysing how European writers and scholars constructed an exotic, irrational and unchanging “Orient”, linked to colonial rule.

fuentes/orientalismo/por_que_importa.texto: It founded postcolonial studies and sparked a debate that is still open, especially with Bernard Lewis.

fuentes/raices-de-la-rabia-musulmana/res.texto: Essay in The Atlantic that explains Islamist anti-Westernism as the reaction of a formerly dominant civilization to its humiliation, and already speaks of a “clash of civilizations”.

fuentes/choque-de-civilizaciones/resumen.texto: After the Cold War, the major conflicts would be between civilizations defined above all by religion; Islam would have “bloody borders”.

fuentes/historia-de-las-cruzadas-runcima.texto: Narrative history in three volumes from the Byzantine perspective, which ends by judging the holy war as “a long act of intolerance in the name of God”.

fuentes/cruzadas-vistas-por-los-arabes/r.texto: Account of the Crusades based on the Arab chroniclers, with the thesis that the trauma of the Frankish invasions shaped the Arab world's relationship with the West.

fuentes/cruzadas-perspectivas-islamicas/.texto: Study of how Muslims experienced, explained and remembered the Crusades: the revival of jihad, the image of the Franks and modern memory.

fuentes/primeras-conquistas-islamicas/re.texto: Explains the conquests by the creation in Arabia of a new state, which channelled the tribes outwards, rather than by the weakness of Byzantium and Persia.

fuentes/grandes-conquistas-arabes/resume.texto: History of the Arab expansion of the 7th and early 8th centuries, from the Atlantic to Central Asia, drawing on Arabic and non-Arabic sources.

fuentes/primera-cruzada-y-la-idea/titulo.texto: The First Crusade and the Idea of Crusading

fuentes/primera-cruzada-y-la-idea/resume.texto: Study of how clerics turned the First Crusade into a theology: an armed pilgrimage and a form of penance for the laity.

fuentes/guerra-de-dios/resumen.texto: General history of the Crusades as a phenomenon of European society, with their financing, their propaganda and their critics.

fuentes/bajo-la-media-luna-y-la-cruz/res.texto: Comparison of the condition of Jews in Christian Europe and in medieval Islam: generally safer under Islam, without the myth of an idyllic coexistence or that of permanent persecution.

fuentes/el-despertar-arabe/resumen.texto: First history of Arab nationalism, written in Jerusalem by a Lebanese-Egyptian intellectual; it was the first to publish the Hussein–McMahon correspondence.

fuentes/origen-del-problema-de-los-refug.texto: The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem
Study based on Israeli archives that showed that the Palestinian exodus resulted from the war, from expulsions and from attacks, and not from Arab orders to flee or from a general plan of expulsion.
It launched the school of the Israeli “new historians”.

fuentes/identidad-palestina/resumen.texto: Study of the emergence of Palestinian national consciousness from the late Ottoman period, based on the press, notable families and local institutions.

fuentes/jerusalen-la-biografia/resumen.texto: History of Jerusalem from David to 1967 through its conquerors, its prophets and its inhabitants.

fuentes/ihya-ulum-al-din/titulo.texto: The Revival of the Religious Sciences

fuentes/ihya-ulum-al-din/resumen.texto: Compendium of some forty books, in four parts of ten (acts of worship, customs of daily life, the vices that condemn and the virtues that save), showing how the doctrine and practices of Islam can be the basis of a deeply devout life, up to the highest stages of Sufism. Al-Ghazali wrote it after leaving, in a spiritual crisis, his chair at the Nizamiyya in Baghdad, and after traveling through Damascus, Jerusalem and Mecca.

fuentes/ihya-ulum-al-din/por_que_importa.texto: It is usually considered the most influential book in Islam after the Quran and the canonical collections of hadith. It joins law and theology with the Sufi path.

fuentes/alquimia-de-la-felicidad/resumen.texto: Treatise in Persian by al-Ghazali, written shortly before 1105, in four parts of ten chapters (religious duties, salvation, human relations and damnation). It insists on performing the rites of Islam, on the actions that lead to salvation and on avoiding sin, with a mystical emphasis on self-discipline and asceticism. It is shorter than the Ihya and is not a rewriting of it, although the author himself said that it reflects its nature.

fuentes/alquimia-de-la-felicidad/por_que.texto: It is credited with helping to reduce the tensions between scholars and Sufis, who accused each other of neglecting ritual obligations and of getting caught up in disputes over philosophy and theology.

fuentes/cronica-de-eusebio/resumen.texto: Universal chronicle from Abraham to the year 325 (the twenty years of Constantine's reign), in two books: the first gathers extracts from earlier authors, and the second, an innovative list of dates and events in parallel columns, one year per line, which includes the longest surviving list of Olympic victors (776 BC–217 AD). The Greek text is lost: it survives in an Armenian translation, and the second book, complete, in Jerome's Latin version.

fuentes/cronica-de-eusebio/por_que_impor.texto: It set the model for the universal Christian chronicle and influenced later chroniclers: Jacob of Edessa continued it from the year 325, and there are quotations from it in Syriac authors such as Michael the Syrian. It was composed before the Ecclesiastical History.

fuentes/cronica-de-eusebio/leer.0.titulo.texto: Jerome's Chronicle (Latin version of Eusebius's), English translation by Roger Pearse

fuentes/de-viris-illustribus/resumen.texto: Latin bibliographical collection written in Bethlehem in 392–393, with a preface and 135 chapters giving a short account of each Christian author and a list of his writings, from the age of the apostles down to Jerome himself. He dedicated it to Nummius Aemilianus Dexter, who had asked him for the survey, and presented it as a Christian counterpart to the catalogs of Suetonius and other classical authors; much of the first part is taken, with few changes, from Eusebius of Caesarea.

fuentes/de-viris-illustribus/por_que_imp.texto: It is a defense of Christian culture and a catalog of the Christian writers of the first centuries. Modern criticism judges it hasty and incomplete, praising or insulting according to what Jerome thought of each author; it was continued by Gennadius of Marseilles and Isidore of Seville.

fuentes/teofanes-continuado/resumen.texto: Four works gathered in an 11th-century manuscript (Vat. gr. 167) that continue Theophanes' Chronographia from 813 to 961: biographies of the emperors from 813 to 867 (from Leo the Armenian to Michael III), commissioned by Constantine VII; the Life of Basil I, written by his grandson Constantine VII around 950; a history from 886 to 948 and its continuation to 961, probably by Theodore Daphnopates.

fuentes/teofanes-continuado/por_que_impo.texto: It covers the years of the sack of Amorium by al-Mu'tasim and of the Byzantine recovery against the Arabs. Since Constantine VII commissioned it, it reflects the viewpoint of the Macedonian dynasty: the Life of Basil is a panegyric that praises Basil and disparages his predecessor, Michael III.

fuentes/militia-dei/resumen.texto: Papal bull of 7 April 1145 that consolidated the independence of the Templars from the local ecclesiastical hierarchy: it gave them the right to collect tithes and burial fees, to bury their dead in their own cemeteries and to move freely through Europe.

fuentes/militia-dei/por_que_importa.texto: Together with Omne datum optimum (1139) and Milites Templi, it laid the basis for the future wealth and success of the order.

fuentes/hexapla/resumen.texto: Critical edition of the Old Testament in six columns: the Hebrew text, the Hebrew in Greek letters, the Greek translations of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, and the Septuagint, with marks showing the additions and omissions in the latter relative to the Hebrew; in the Psalms there were three more versions. It was lost, and fragments survive, gathered above all by Frederick Field (1875). Uncertain date: between about 212, when Origen is said to have begun it, and before 240.

fuentes/hexapla/por_que_importa.texto: It is the first critical edition of the Bible and the source of what is known of several lost Greek translations. Modern specialists do not agree on its purpose: whether to facilitate debate and translation, or to recover the original or oldest text. Its only copy remained in the library at Caesarea.

fuentes/tafsir-al-tabari/titulo.texto: Collection of explanations of the interpretation of the verses of the Quran

fuentes/tafsir-al-tabari/resumen.texto: Sunni commentary on the Quran, verse by verse, which for each passage gathers several accounts, often contradictory, with their chains of transmitters and, at times, al-Tabari's judgment on their reliability. He finished it in 883; The History of the Prophets and Kings, his other major work, he completed around 915.

fuentes/tafsir-al-tabari/por_que_importa.texto: It is the first great continuous commentary on the Quran to survive in its original form, and it is still highly valued by specialists. A group of scholars from Transoxiana translated it into Persian at the request of the Samanid Mansur I (961-976).

fuentes/ketubot/resumen.texto: Tractate of the Nashim (“women”) order of the Mishnah and the Talmud, on the obligations of marriage and, above all, the Jewish marriage contract (the ketubah), which sets out the rights and duties of the groom toward the bride. It has thirteen chapters and, given the breadth of its subjects, is called “the small Talmud” (shas katan). The Mishnah text is attributed to the compilation of Judah ha-Nasi (around 200); the Gemara of the Babylonian Talmud on this tractate was compiled with the rest of the Talmud, between the 5th and 6th centuries.

fuentes/ketubot/por_que_importa.texto: It shows how oral law regulated marriage and the rights of the wife and the widow. The ketubah still has legal force in Israel today.

fuentes/ivanhoe/resumen.texto: Historical novel in three volumes (December 1819), set in England in 1194, when the crusaders were returning from the Third Crusade. Wilfred of Ivanhoe, who accompanied Richard the Lionheart to the Holy Land, returns in disguise to an England of tournaments, outlaws, a witchcraft trial, and the divisions between Jews and Christians and between Normans and Saxons; the novel features the Templar Brian de Bois-Guilbert and the Jewish woman Rebecca, daughter of Isaac of York.

fuentes/ivanhoe/por_que_importa.texto: It was Scott's most popular work. It is credited with reviving interest in chivalry and medievalism (Carlyle and Ruskin) and with shaping the popular image of Richard I, Prince John and Robin Hood.

fuentes/los-cuatro-libros/resumen.texto: The four canonical collections of hadith of Twelver Shiism: al-Kafi, by al-Kulayni (d. 941); Man la yahduruhu al-faqih, by Ibn Babawayh (al-Saduq); and Tahdhib al-ahkam and al-Istibsar, by al-Tusi. Twelver Shiites regard the Prophet and the twelve imams as the absolute authority of the religion, so much of their hadith is transmitted through the imams, and they judge many Sunni transmitters unreliable because of their attitude toward the Ahl al-Bayt, the family of the Prophet.

fuentes/los-cuatro-libros/por_que_import.texto: For Shiism they are what the six canonical books (Kutub al-Sitta) are for Sunnism, and they preserve what that tradition knows of Ali, Husayn and the imams. Twelver Shiites do not use the six Sunni collections.

fuentes/opinion-consultiva-cij-2004-muro.texto: Legal Consequences of the Construction of a Wall in the Occupied Palestinian Territory

Advisory opinion issued by the International Court of Justice on 9 July 2004, at the request of the UN General Assembly. It concluded that the sections of the wall that Israel is building inside the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and the associated permit regime violate Israel's obligations under international law. Israel argued that the barrier was necessary to prevent attacks and rejected the Court's jurisdiction and the opinion.
The Court held that the wall inside the West Bank should be dismantled; Israel rejected the opinion.
Case file and text of the opinion on the website of the International Court of Justice

fuentes/opinion-consultiva-cij-2024-ocup.texto: Legal Consequences arising from the Policies and Practices of Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem

Advisory opinion issued by the International Court of Justice on 19 July 2024, at the request of the UN General Assembly. It held that Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory (the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza) is unlawful, that it must end as soon as possible, and that Israel must make reparation for the damage. The government of Israel rejected the opinion and said that a solution can only come from negotiations.

The Court rejected the Israeli thesis that Gaza ceased to be occupied after 2005. In September 2024 the General Assembly passed a resolution calling for Israel's unlawful presence to end within one year.
Case file and text of the opinion on the website of the International Court of Justice

fuentes/resolucion-487/resumen.texto: Resolution adopted unanimously on 19 June 1981. It condemned the Israeli attack on an Iraqi nuclear facility approved by the IAEA, called for an end to hostilities, recognized Iraq's right to claim compensation, and urged Israel to place its nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards.

fuentes/resolucion-487/por_que_importa.texto: It is the Security Council's response to Operation Opera.

fuentes/resolucion-487/leer.0.titulo.texto: Official text in the UN document system

fuentes/resolucion-573/resumen.texto: Resolution adopted on 4 October 1985, with 14 votes in favor and the abstention of the United States, after a complaint from Tunisia. It condemned the Israeli air strike of 1 October, reminded states that they must refrain from the threat or use of force, demanded that Israel refrain from further attacks, and recognized Tunisia's right to reparation.

fuentes/resolucion-573/por_que_importa.texto: It is the Security Council's response to Operation Wooden Leg.

fuentes/resolucion-1701/resumen.texto: Resolution adopted unanimously on 11 August 2006 to end the Lebanon war. It called for a cessation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah, the withdrawal of Israeli forces, that south of the Litani River there be no armed forces other than the Lebanese army and UNIFIL, and the disarmament of armed groups.

fuentes/resolucion-1701/por_que_importa.texto: It is the framework for the later truces along the border. Lebanon accuses Israel of not withdrawing from some territories and of violating its airspace, and Israel accuses Hezbollah of not withdrawing from south of the Litani.

fuentes/iniciativa-de-paz-arabe/resumen.texto: Ten-sentence proposal presented by Saudi Crown Prince Abdullah and adopted by the Arab League at the Beirut summit of 2002. It offers normalization of relations between the Arab countries and Israel in exchange for its full withdrawal from the occupied territories, an agreed solution for the Palestinian refugees under resolution 194, and a Palestinian state with its capital in East Jerusalem.

fuentes/iniciativa-de-paz-arabe/por_que_.texto: The Arab League reaffirmed it in 2007 and 2017. Sharon's government rejected it; Netanyahu expressed tentative support in 2015 and rejected it as a basis for negotiation in 2018.

personas/david/resumen.texto: King of Israel and Judah according to the Bible, which presents him as a shepherd, musician and warrior who took Jerusalem and founded the dynasty from which the messiah was expected. The Tel Dan stele, from the 9th century BC, names the “House of David”; the actual extent of his kingdom is debated.

personas/salomon/resumen.texto: Son of David, a wise king and builder of the First Temple in Jerusalem according to the Bible, which attributes to him Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs. He is also a prophet in the Quran (Sulayman).

personas/ezequias/resumen.texto: King of Judah who withstood the Assyrian siege by Sennacherib in 701 BC and had the Siloam tunnel dug to bring water inside the walls. His royal seal was found in Jerusalem in 2015.

personas/esdras/resumen.texto: Scribe who, according to the Bible, returned from Babylon with the law of Moses and had it read publicly in Jerusalem. Jewish tradition credits him with fixing the Torah and with the shift to the Aramaic square script.

personas/antioco-iv/resumen.texto: Seleucid king who in 167 BC banned circumcision and the Sabbath and dedicated the Temple in Jerusalem to Olympian Zeus. His persecution provoked the Maccabean revolt and left its mark on the Book of Daniel.

personas/judas-macabeo/resumen.texto: Son of the priest Mattathias and leader of the revolt against the Seleucids. He recovered the Temple in 164 BC, an event remembered in the festival of Hanukkah, and died at the battle of Elasa.

personas/hilel/resumen.texto: Babylonian teacher who settled in Jerusalem and founded the more flexible school of legal interpretation. He is credited with summing up the Torah as “what you do not want for yourself, do not do to your neighbor; the rest is commentary.”

personas/filon/resumen.texto: Jewish philosopher who read the Torah through the categories of Plato and the Stoics by means of allegory, and spoke of the Logos as mediator between God and the world. His method passed to the Church Fathers of Alexandria.

personas/jesus/resumen.texto: Jewish preacher from Galilee who announced the coming of the kingdom of God and was crucified in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate. His followers proclaimed him the risen messiah (Christ), and Christianity grew out of that movement; the Quran reveres him as a prophet and messiah but denies his divinity and his crucifixion.

personas/yohanan-ben-zakai/resumen.texto: According to tradition, he left besieged Jerusalem hidden in a coffin and obtained permission from Vespasian to open an academy at Yavne. There Judaism rebuilt itself without the Temple, around study and prayer.

personas/rabi-akiva/resumen.texto: The most influential of the sages of the Mishnah, who organized the oral law. He supported Bar Kokhba as messiah and, according to the Talmud, died tortured by the Romans while reciting the Shema.

personas/bar-kojba/resumen.texto: Leader of the last great Jewish revolt against Rome, whom Rabbi Akiva hailed as messiah. His letters were found in caves in the Judean Desert; the defeat at Betar ended the Jewish majority presence in Judea.

personas/tito/resumen.texto: Son of Vespasian, he took Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple in 70. His triumphal arch in Rome shows the plundering of the Temple menorah.

personas/adriano/resumen.texto: He refounded Jerusalem as a Roman colony, Aelia Capitolina, which set off the revolt of Bar Kokhba. After crushing it he barred the city to Jews and renamed the province of Judea as Syria Palaestina. In Britain he ordered the wall that bears his name to be built from 122 onward.

personas/juda-ha-nasi/resumen.texto: Patriarch of the Jews of Palestine, recognized by Rome, who compiled the oral law and set it down in writing in the Mishnah c. 200. In rabbinic literature he is simply “Rabbi.”

personas/origenes/resumen.texto: Alexandrian theologian who settled in Caesarea, where he assembled a great library and compared the Hebrew text and the Greek translations of the Bible in the Hexapla. He combined Christian faith with Platonism; he died from torture suffered in the persecution of Decius.

personas/eusebio/resumen.texto: Bishop of Caesarea, father of church history and biographer of Constantine. His Onomasticon is the first geography of biblical places.

personas/constantino-i/resumen.texto: The first Christian emperor, who legalized Christianity in 313 and presided over the Council of Nicaea. He had the Holy Sepulchre and other basilicas built, through which Palestine became the Holy Land of Christians.

personas/helena/resumen.texto: Mother of Constantine. Her pilgrimage to Palestine in 326 gave rise to the Church of the Nativity and the basilica on the Mount of Olives; later tradition credits her with finding the True Cross.

personas/cirilo-de-jerusalen/resumen.texto: Bishop of Jerusalem whose catechetical lectures, delivered in the Holy Sepulchre, are the best testimony to the city's liturgy in the 4th century.

personas/juliano/resumen.texto: Last pagan emperor, educated in Neoplatonism. In 363 he ordered the Temple in Jerusalem rebuilt to disprove Christian prophecies, but the work was abandoned after a fire and his death in Persia.

personas/egeria/resumen.texto: A woman from Hispania or Gaul who made a pilgrimage to Egypt, Sinai, Palestine and Mesopotamia and wrote an account in Latin to her “sisters,” the earliest surviving account by a woman pilgrim.

personas/jeronimo/resumen.texto: Scholar from Dalmatia who learned Hebrew from Jewish teachers and lived 34 years in a monastery in Bethlehem. There he translated almost the whole Bible into Latin from the Hebrew: the Vulgate, the text of the Latin Church for a thousand years. Earlier he had studied in Trier and passed through Ancyra, and in his commentary on the Letter to the Galatians (around 387) he wrote that the Galatians spoke almost the same language as the Treveri.

personas/cosroes-ii/resumen.texto: Sasanian king whose war against Byzantium brought the Persians into Syria, Palestine and Egypt. His troops took Jerusalem in 614 and carried off the True Cross; Heraclius defeated him, and he was deposed and executed in 628.

personas/heraclio/resumen.texto: He defeated Persia and returned the True Cross to Jerusalem in 630, but within a few years lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt to the Arabs. According to several sources, he ordered the forced baptism of the Jews of the Empire.

personas/sofronio/resumen.texto: Monk and theologian who, as patriarch, defended Jerusalem during the Arab siege and surrendered it to Caliph Umar. In his Christmas sermon of 634 he lamented that the “Saracens” prevented the faithful from going to Bethlehem.

personas/constantino-iv/resumen.texto: He withstood the first Arab siege of Constantinople (674-678), in which the Byzantine fleet used Greek fire for the first time.

personas/leon-iii/resumen.texto: He withstood the great Arab siege of 717-718, whose failure halted Islamic expansion into eastern Europe for centuries, and began the Iconoclast crisis.

personas/teofanes/resumen.texto: Byzantine monk whose Chronographia, covering 284 to 813, is the main Greek source on Muhammad and the Arab conquests; he calls Muhammad a “false prophet.”

personas/niceforo-ii/resumen.texto: General who reconquered Crete (961), Cyprus (965) and Antioch (969). He asked that soldiers killed fighting the Muslims be honored as martyrs, and the patriarch refused: Byzantium had no idea of holy war like that of the Crusades.

personas/juan-i-tzimisces/resumen.texto: In 975 he led his army through Syria as far as Galilee; in a letter to the king of Armenia, preserved by Matthew of Edessa, he says he wanted to liberate the Holy Sepulchre.

personas/romano-iv/resumen.texto: He was defeated and captured by the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan at Manzikert (1071), which opened Anatolia to the Turks.

personas/alejo-i/resumen.texto: Emperor who saved Byzantium from collapse. His envoys asked the pope for help against the Turks at Piacenza (1095), which Urban II turned into the First Crusade; he then required the crusader leaders to swear an oath to return the Byzantine cities to him.

personas/manuel-i/resumen.texto: Emperor allied with the Crusader States, who married a princess of Antioch. His defeat by the Seljuks at Myriokephalon (1176) halted the recovery of Anatolia.

personas/nicetas-coniates/resumen.texto: High official who witnessed the sack of Constantinople by the crusaders in 1204 and recounted it bitterly: the Saracens, he writes, had been more merciful to Jerusalem than these Christians were to his city.

personas/juan-vi-cantacuceno/resumen.texto: Emperor who, after abdicating in 1354 and becoming a monk, wrote four apologies against Islam and four orations against Muhammad, drawing on Riccoldo's Latin polemic.

personas/manuel-ii/resumen.texto: He traveled through Italy, France and England between 1399 and 1403 seeking help against the Ottomans. His dialogues with a Muslim scholar, written in Ankara in 1391, are the text Benedict XVI quoted in Regensburg in 2006.

personas/juan-viii/resumen.texto: He traveled to the Council of Florence (1438-1439) and accepted the union of the Churches with Rome in order to obtain a crusade, which ended in the disaster of Varna (1444); the union was rejected in Constantinople.

personas/critobulo/resumen.texto: Greek nobleman who entered the service of Mehmed II and wrote his history, dedicated to the sultan, with the conquest of Constantinople as its great deed.

personas/ducas/resumen.texto: Greek historian in the service of the Genoese of Lesbos, author of the most vivid account of the fall of Constantinople.

personas/jorge-esfrantzes/resumen.texto: Friend and minister of the last emperor, Constantine XI. He was captured in the fall of 1453 and ended his days as a monk in Corfu, where he wrote his chronicle.

personas/nicolo-barbaro/resumen.texto: Venetian physician who lived through the siege of 1453 aboard his republic's galleys and kept a day-by-day diary.

personas/mahoma/resumen.texto: Merchant of Mecca who from c. 610 said he received revelations from God through the angel Gabriel, collected in the Quran. Persecuted, he emigrated to Medina in 622, where he was at once prophet, lawgiver and military leader; at his death he had united almost all of Arabia under Islam.

personas/jadiya/resumen.texto: Wealthy merchant of Mecca, Muhammad's first wife and, according to tradition, the first person to believe in his revelation.

personas/abu-bakr/resumen.texto: Father-in-law and companion of Muhammad, the first caliph. He subdued the tribes that broke away after the Prophet's death (the Ridda wars) and launched the first armies toward Syria and Iraq.

personas/omar/resumen.texto: Second caliph: under his rule the Arabs conquered Syria, Palestine, Egypt and almost all of the Persian Empire. He entered Jerusalem in 637 or 638 and, according to Muslim tradition, guaranteed the safety of its inhabitants and allowed the Jews to return; the Pact of Umar is attributed to him, although the known text is later.

personas/uthman/resumen.texto: Third caliph, of the Umayyad family. He had a single text of the Quran fixed and the divergent versions destroyed; his assassination opened the first civil war of Islam.

personas/ali/resumen.texto: Cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad, the fourth caliph. His assassination and that of his son Husayn lie at the origin of the division between Sunnis and Shias, who regard him as the first imam.

personas/jalid/resumen.texto: The most celebrated general of the conquests, called “the Sword of God.” He fought against Muhammad at Uhud and, once a Muslim, led the campaigns in Iraq and Syria.

personas/amr/resumen.texto: Conqueror of Palestine and Egypt, where he founded Fustat, the city from which Cairo grew.

personas/abu-ubayda/resumen.texto: Commander-in-chief of the Arab army in Syria and at the battle of Yarmouk; he died in the plague of Amwas, which killed thousands of Arab soldiers.

personas/muawiya/resumen.texto: Governor of Syria for twenty years and founder of the Umayyad caliphate, with its capital in Damascus. He created the first Arab fleet, attacked Cyprus and Rhodes and besieged Constantinople.

personas/husayn/resumen.texto: Grandson of Muhammad, killed with his family at Karbala when he rebelled against the Umayyad caliph Yazid. His martyrdom, commemorated every year at Ashura, is central to Shia identity.

personas/abd-al-malik/resumen.texto: Umayyad caliph who built the Dome of the Rock, imposed Arabic as the language of administration and minted the first Islamic coins bearing only inscriptions, with verses from the Quran against the Trinity.

personas/al-walid-i/resumen.texto: Caliph at the height of Umayyad expansion, from Hispania to the Indus. He built the Umayyad Mosque of Damascus and enlarged the mosques of Medina and al-Aqsa.

personas/uqba/resumen.texto: Conqueror of the Maghreb and founder of Kairouan (670). According to tradition he reached the Atlantic; he died in an ambush by the Berber leader Kusaila.

personas/kahina/resumen.texto: Berber queen of the Aurès, called al-Kahina (“the soothsayer”) by the Arabs, who defeated their armies and resisted until she died in battle c. 703. She is a figure of Berber memory and of Algerian nationalism.

personas/musa-ibn-nusayr/resumen.texto: Governor of Ifriqiya who completed the conquest of the Maghreb and led that of Hispania from 712, after the landing of his lieutenant Tariq.

personas/tariq/resumen.texto: Berber leader who crossed the strait in 711 and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic at Guadalete. Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq, “the mountain of Tariq”) bears his name.

personas/harun-al-rashid/resumen.texto: Abbasid caliph of the Thousand and One Nights. He exchanged embassies with Charlemagne, who according to Einhard received from him an elephant and symbolic keys to the Holy Sepulchre.

personas/al-mamun/resumen.texto: Abbasid caliph who promoted translations from Greek at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad and imposed the rationalist Mu'tazilite theology by force.

personas/al-hakim/resumen.texto: Fatimid caliph who ordered the destruction of the Holy Sepulchre in 1009 and persecuted Christians and Jews. The Druze regard him as a manifestation of God.

personas/alp-arslan/resumen.texto: Seljuk sultan who defeated and captured Romanos IV at Manzikert (1071) and released him for a ransom.

personas/pedro-el-ermitano/resumen.texto: Preacher from Amiens who drew thousands of peasants into the People's Crusade of 1096, wiped out by the Turks in Anatolia; he then followed the main army to Jerusalem.

personas/emicho/resumen.texto: Rhineland count who led the band of crusaders that in May 1096 massacred the Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms and Mainz, before being broken up in Hungary.

personas/godofredo/resumen.texto: Duke of Lower Lorraine and leader of the First Crusade. After the capture of Jerusalem he agreed to rule it, but according to tradition he refused to wear a crown of gold where Christ had worn one of thorns and took the title of Defender of the Holy Sepulchre.

personas/balduino-i/resumen.texto: Brother of Godfrey, first count of Edessa (1098) and first king of Jerusalem (1100), who conquered almost the entire coast.

personas/bohemundo/resumen.texto: Norman from southern Italy who kept Antioch for himself in 1098, against the oath sworn to Alexios I, and founded a principality there.

personas/raimundo-de-tolosa/resumen.texto: The richest of the leaders of the First Crusade, who traveled with the papal legate. He died besieging Tripoli, which would become the capital of the county founded by his family.

personas/ademar/resumen.texto: Bishop of Le Puy and legate of Urban II on the First Crusade; he died of plague in Antioch.

personas/tancredo/resumen.texto: Nephew of Bohemond, prince of Galilee and regent of Antioch. Tasso made him the protagonist of Jerusalem Delivered.

personas/hugo-de-payns/resumen.texto: Knight from Champagne who c. 1119, with other companions, founded the Order of the Temple to protect pilgrims; he obtained its rule at the Council of Troyes (1129) with the support of Bernard of Clairvaux.

personas/melisenda/resumen.texto: Queen of Jerusalem in her own right, daughter of a Frank and an Armenian. She ruled with her husband and later with her son, and was a patron of churches and of the psalter that bears her name.

personas/balduino-iv/resumen.texto: The “leper king,” who at sixteen defeated Saladin at Montgisard (1177) and ruled, increasingly ill, until his death.

personas/reinaldo-de-chatillon/resumen.texto: Lord of Kerak who attacked caravans during truces and in 1182-1183 sent a fleet down the Red Sea toward the holy cities of Islam. Saladin executed him with his own hand after Hattin.

personas/guido-de-lusinan/resumen.texto: King of Jerusalem defeated and captured at Hattin (1187). Once freed, he besieged Acre and ended up buying Cyprus, where his family reigned for three centuries.

personas/balian-de-ibelin/resumen.texto: Frankish noble born in the East who defended Jerusalem in 1187 and negotiated its surrender with Saladin, with a ransom for each inhabitant.

personas/conrado-de-montferrato/resumen.texto: He saved Tyre after Hattin and was elected king of Jerusalem in 1192, but was assassinated by two Nizaris days later.

personas/ricardo-i/resumen.texto: King of England and leader of the Third Crusade. He conquered Cyprus, took Acre, had some 2,700 Muslim prisoners killed at Ayyadieh and won at Arsuf, but did not attempt to take Jerusalem and signed a truce with Saladin in 1192.

personas/eugenio-iii/resumen.texto: Cistercian pope, a disciple of Bernard of Clairvaux, who called the Second Crusade after the fall of Edessa with the bull Quantum praedecessores (1145).

personas/pedro-el-venerable/resumen.texto: Abbot of Cluny who, on a journey to Spain (1142), commissioned the first Latin translation of the Quran and of other Islamic texts. He wanted to refute Islam with arguments rather than arms: “not with arms, but with words; not with force, but with reason.”

personas/roberto-de-ketton/resumen.texto: English translator of Arabic scientific texts who made, for Peter the Venerable, the first Latin translation of the Quran (1143), a paraphrase that was read in Europe for five centuries.

personas/fulquerio/resumen.texto: Chaplain of Baldwin I who heard Urban II at Clermont and lived in Jerusalem. His chronicle follows the kingdom until 1127 and celebrates that the Franks have become “Orientals.”

personas/raimundo-de-aguilers/resumen.texto: Chaplain of Raymond of Toulouse and eyewitness to the First Crusade. He describes the massacre of Jerusalem, with blood up to the knees, as a judgment of God.

personas/guiberto-de-nogent/resumen.texto: Benedictine abbot who rewrote the history of the First Crusade as the work of God through the Franks. He also wrote one of the first medieval autobiographies and a life of Muhammad full of legends.

personas/alberto-de-aquisgran/resumen.texto: Cleric of Aachen who, without having gone to the East, wrote the most detailed chronicle of the First Crusade based on witnesses, including the massacres of Jews in the Rhineland.

personas/guillermo-de-tiro/resumen.texto: Archbishop born in Jerusalem, educated in Paris and Bologna, chancellor of the kingdom and tutor of Baldwin IV. His history of the Crusader States, written with Arabic sources and documents, is the finest Latin historical work of the 12th century.

personas/riccoldo/resumen.texto: Dominican friar who made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land and lived for years in Baghdad, where he studied the Quran in Arabic. His Contra legem Sarracenorum was the most widely read refutation of Islam in Europe; Luther translated it into German.

personas/pierre-dubois/resumen.texto: Norman lawyer in the service of Philip IV who in 1306 proposed recovering the Holy Land through a Europe pacified under the king of France, a court of arbitration between princes, and schools of Oriental languages, also open to women.

personas/marino-sanudo/resumen.texto: Venetian noble who presented the pope in 1321 with a crusade plan based on the economic blockade of Egypt, with maps by Pietro Vesconte.

personas/humberto-de-romans/resumen.texto: Master General of the Dominicans who, for the Council of Lyon of 1274, wrote a treatise in defense of the crusade that sets out and answers the objections of its critics.

personas/felix-fabri/resumen.texto: Friar from Ulm who made two pilgrimages to Jerusalem and Sinai and wrote the longest and most detailed travel account of the Middle Ages.

personas/pio-ii/resumen.texto: Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, humanist and pope, who devoted his pontificate to a crusade against the Ottomans after the fall of Constantinople. He wrote to Mehmed II proposing that he convert, and died in Ancona waiting for a fleet that never arrived.

personas/lutero/resumen.texto: The German reformer saw the Turks as a punishment from God and, in On War Against the Turk (1529), argued that the war should be waged by the emperor and not by the Church as a crusade. He translated Riccoldo's refutation and supported Bibliander's edition of the Quran.

personas/erasmo/resumen.texto: The most widely read humanist of his time criticized the Crusades as a business of popes and princes, although in 1530 he accepted a defensive war against the Turks if waged in a Christian spirit.

personas/bibliander/resumen.texto: Zurich theologian who published in Basel (1543) Robert of Ketton's Latin translation of the Quran with polemical texts, after a lawsuit with the city council that had banned it.

personas/tasso/resumen.texto: Italian poet whose Jerusalem Delivered (1581) turned the First Crusade into an epic of the Counter-Reformation, with love affairs between crusaders and Muslim warrior women.

personas/voltaire/resumen.texto: In his tragedy Mahomet, or Fanaticism (1741) he used the Prophet as a figure of religious fanaticism; in the Essay on Manners he was more nuanced, praising the tolerance of the caliphs and criticizing the Crusades.

personas/lessing/resumen.texto: His Nathan the Wise (1779), set in the Jerusalem of the Third Crusade, brings together a Jew, Saladin and a Templar; the parable of the three rings is the great Enlightenment plea for tolerance between religions.

personas/gibbon/resumen.texto: English historian whose History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire devotes famous chapters to Muhammad, the Arab conquests and the Crusades, with irony toward the fanaticism of all sides.

personas/volney/resumen.texto: Enlightenment philosopher who traveled through Egypt and Syria (1783-1785) and wrote an unromantic description of the region under the Ottomans, read by Napoleon before his expedition.

personas/goethe/resumen.texto: In the West-Eastern Divan (1819), inspired by Hafez, the German poet celebrated Persian and Islamic poetry as a counterpart in dialogue with Europe.

personas/chateaubriand/resumen.texto: Romantic writer who made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem in 1806 and wrote the Itinerary from Paris to Jerusalem (1811), which defends the Crusades as a struggle of Christian civilization.

personas/walter-scott/resumen.texto: His novel The Talisman (1825) portrayed Saladin as a knight nobler than many crusaders, an image that became popular in Europe.

personas/lamartine/resumen.texto: Romantic poet who traveled to the East in 1832–1833 and wrote the Voyage en Orient; later, a History of Turkey with an admiring portrait of Muhammad.

personas/carlyle/resumen.texto: In the lecture “The Hero as Prophet” (1840) he defended Muhammad’s sincerity against the tradition that depicted him as an impostor.

personas/renan/resumen.texto: Philologist and philosopher who travelled through Palestine and wrote the Life of Jesus (1863). In his 1883 lecture on Islam and science he argued that Islam was hostile to science, which provoked the response of al-Afghani. In The Poetry of the Celtic Races (1854) he fixed the romantic image of the Celt as a dreamy, melancholy and defeated figure, which Matthew Arnold later took up.

personas/mark-twain/resumen.texto: He traveled to the Holy Land in 1867 on the first American tourist cruise and wrote The Innocents Abroad (1869), with ironic descriptions of a poor and desolate Palestine that were widely quoted later.

personas/ibn-ishaq/resumen.texto: Author of the first major biography of Muhammad, preserved in Ibn Hisham’s edition and in quotations by other authors.

personas/bujari/resumen.texto: He traveled across the Islamic world collecting sayings of Muhammad and selected some 7,000 that he judged authentic; for Sunnis his Sahih is the most reliable book after the Quran.

personas/al-baladuri/resumen.texto: Historian at the Abbasid court, author of the Book of the Conquests of Lands, the classic account of the Arab expansion region by region.

personas/al-tabari/resumen.texto: Author of the great commentary on the Quran and of a universal history up to 915, which records, with their chains of transmitters, every version of each event he found.

personas/al-farabi/resumen.texto: The “second teacher” after Aristotle. In The Virtuous City, completed in Damascus, he joined Plato’s politics with prophecy: the prophet-lawgiver as philosopher-king.

personas/al-muqaddasi/resumen.texto: Geographer born in Jerusalem who traveled across the Islamic world and wrote a description of its provinces, with pages of pride in his native city, where, he complains, Christians and Jews were the majority.

personas/nasir-jusraw/resumen.texto: Persian poet and Ismaili missionary who visited Jerusalem in 1047 and described the Fatimid city, the rebuilt Holy Sepulchre and the pilgrimage of Muslims who could not go to Mecca.

personas/al-gazali/resumen.texto: Theologian who attacked philosophy in The Incoherence of the Philosophers and then, in crisis, left his teaching post in Baghdad in 1095 to live as a Sufi in Damascus and Jerusalem. His works do not mention the arrival of the crusaders, who took Jerusalem a few years later.

personas/al-sulami/resumen.texto: Damascene jurist who in 1105 dictated the Book of Jihad in the Great Mosque, the first call to holy war against the crusaders. He saw the crusade as part of a Christian offensive that included Sicily and al-Andalus.

personas/ibn-al-qalanisi/resumen.texto: Mayor of Damascus and author of its chronicle, the only contemporary Arabic account of the First Crusade.

personas/usama/resumen.texto: Syrian emir who fought the Franks and dealt with them as a diplomat. His memoirs depict the crusaders with curiosity and contempt: their brutal medicine, their ordeals, and also Templars who defended him so that he could pray in peace.

personas/zengi/resumen.texto: Turkish atabeg of Mosul and Aleppo who took Edessa in 1144, the first major crusader defeat, and was celebrated as a champion of jihad.

personas/nur-al-din/resumen.texto: Son of Zengi, he united Muslim Syria and turned jihad into a program of government: madrasas, propaganda, a pulpit made for Jerusalem before recovering it. He sent Saladin to Egypt.

personas/ibn-asakir/resumen.texto: Damascene scholar in the service of Nur al-Din, author of an eighty-volume history of the city and of collections of sayings of Muhammad on jihad and the merits of Jerusalem.

personas/imad-al-din/resumen.texto: Secretary to Nur al-Din and Saladin, author of the account of the reconquest of Jerusalem in 1187 in rhymed prose.

personas/baha-al-din/resumen.texto: Judge of Saladin’s army and his biographer, who portrays him as a model of piety and jihad; he witnessed Hattin, Acre and Arsuf.

personas/ibn-al-athir/resumen.texto: Historian of Mosul whose Complete History narrates the crusades from the Muslim side and criticizes the divisions among the princes. He also described the terror of the Mongol invasion.

personas/al-kamil/resumen.texto: Ayyubid sultan of Egypt, nephew of Saladin. He received Francis of Assisi at Damietta in 1219 and in 1229 handed Jerusalem over to Frederick II by treaty, without war.

personas/baibars/resumen.texto: Kipchak slave who became Mamluk sultan, victor over the Mongols at Ain Jalut and destroyer of the Crusader States: Caesarea, Jaffa, Antioch and the Krak fell to him.

personas/al-ashraf-jalil/resumen.texto: Mamluk sultan who took Acre in 1291 and with it the last remnants of the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

personas/abulfeda/resumen.texto: Ayyubid prince who as a young man fought in the capture of Acre (1291) and, as emir of Hama, wrote a universal history and a geography that were later widely read in Europe.

personas/ibn-taymiyya/resumen.texto: Hanbali jurist who called for jihad against the Mongols even though they declared themselves Muslims, because they did not govern according to Islamic law. His ideas on jihad and on when a ruler ceases to be Muslim are a central reference of modern Islamism.

personas/ibn-battuta/resumen.texto: Traveler from Tangier who over almost thirty years journeyed from the Maghreb to China; he passed through Jerusalem, Damascus and Mecca in 1326.

personas/ibn-jaldun/resumen.texto: Historian and thinker from Tunis. In the Muqaddimah he explained the rise and fall of dynasties through the group cohesion (asabiyya) of the nomadic peoples who conquer cities. He met Tamerlane outside Damascus in 1401.

personas/mujir-al-din/resumen.texto: Judge of Jerusalem who wrote in 1496 a history of Jerusalem and Hebron, with the most complete description of the Mamluk city.

personas/selim-i/resumen.texto: Ottoman sultan who defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq (1516) and conquered Syria, Palestine, Egypt and the protectorship of Mecca and Medina.

personas/soliman/resumen.texto: Sultan who brought the Ottoman Empire to its height: he took Belgrade and Rhodes, won at Mohács and besieged Vienna. He rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem that still surround it.

personas/benjamin-de-tudela/resumen.texto: Navarrese Jewish traveler who between 1165 and 1173 visited the Jewish communities of the Mediterranean and the East; in Jerusalem, he says, only a few families of dyers remained.

personas/obadia-de-bertinoro/resumen.texto: Italian rabbi who settled in Jerusalem in 1488 and reorganized its poor community. His letters describe the Mamluk city, and his commentary on the Mishnah is still printed in every edition.

personas/joseph-caro/resumen.texto: Born in Toledo shortly before the expulsion, he settled in Safed. His Shulchan Aruch (1563) is still the code of Jewish law.

personas/moises-cordovero/resumen.texto: The great systematizer of Safed Kabbalah before Luria, author of the Orchard of Pomegranates.

personas/isaac-luria/resumen.texto: The “holy lion” of Safed. His Kabbalah, transmitted by his disciples, explains creation as God’s contraction (tzimtzum), the breaking of the vessels and the repair of the world (tikkun) through human actions.

personas/jaim-vital/resumen.texto: Luria’s chief disciple, who put his teaching in writing in the Tree of Life.

personas/shlomo-alkabetz/resumen.texto: Safed kabbalist, author of the hymn Lekhah Dodi with which Jews all over the world welcome the Sabbath.

personas/gracia-mendes/resumen.texto: Portuguese converso banker who fled the Inquisition to Istanbul. With her nephew Joseph Nasi she obtained from Suleiman the lease of Tiberias to settle Jews there, an early project of return.

personas/sabetai-zevi/resumen.texto: Kabbalist from Smyrna proclaimed messiah in Gaza in 1665 by Nathan of Gaza; he stirred Jewish communities from Poland to Yemen. Arrested by the sultan, he converted to Islam in 1666.

personas/natan-de-gaza/resumen.texto: Young kabbalist who proclaimed Sabbatai Zevi messiah and later explained his apostasy as a necessary descent into evil in order to redeem it.

personas/moses-montefiore/resumen.texto: British banker and philanthropist who traveled seven times to the Holy Land and in 1860 built outside the walls of Jerusalem the first new Jewish neighborhood, Mishkenot Sha'ananim.

personas/moses-hess/resumen.texto: Socialist and friend of Marx who in Rome and Jerusalem (1862) proposed a socialist Jewish state in Palestine, a precursor of Zionism.

personas/leon-pinsker/resumen.texto: Odessa physician who after the pogroms of 1881 wrote Auto-Emancipation: Jews would not be accepted in Europe and needed a land of their own.

personas/eliezer-ben-yehuda/resumen.texto: Lexicographer who arrived in Jerusalem in 1881 and set out to make Hebrew a spoken language again: he raised his son only in Hebrew and wrote a great dictionary of ancient and modern Hebrew.

personas/ahad-haam/resumen.texto: Thinker of cultural Zionism, who wanted a spiritual center of the Jewish people in Palestine rather than a state. In “Truth from the Land of Israel” (1891) he warned that the land was not empty and that the Arabs had to be treated with respect.

personas/herzl/resumen.texto: Viennese journalist who, after the Dreyfus affair, wrote The Jewish State (1896) and convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel (1897). He founded political Zionism, which sought a state recognized by the powers.

personas/weizmann/resumen.texto: Chemist at the University of Manchester and Zionist leader who obtained the Balfour Declaration (1917) and signed an agreement with Emir Faisal in 1919. He was the first president of Israel.

personas/jabotinsky/resumen.texto: Founder of Revisionist Zionism. In “The Iron Wall” (1923) he argued that the Arabs would not accept a Jewish majority of their own free will and that only a Jewish military force would bring them to negotiate.

personas/abraham-kook/resumen.texto: First Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Palestine, mystic and philosopher, who saw secular Zionism as an instrument of redemption; his thought inspires religious Zionism.

personas/martin-buber/resumen.texto: Philosopher of dialogue (I and Thou, 1923) and critical Zionist, who with Brit Shalom advocated a binational Jewish-Arab state. He emigrated to Jerusalem in 1938.

personas/gershom-scholem/resumen.texto: Founder of the academic study of Jewish mysticism, with books on Kabbalah, Luria and Sabbatai Zevi.

personas/ben-gurion/resumen.texto: Labor leader of the Zionist movement, who proclaimed Israel’s independence on May 14, 1948, and was its first head of government.

personas/golda-meir/resumen.texto: Born in Kyiv and raised in the United States, prime minister of Israel during the Yom Kippur War (1973).

personas/begin/resumen.texto: Head of the Irgun, an armed group that blew up the King David Hotel in 1946. As prime minister he signed peace with Egypt (1979) and shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Sadat.

personas/rabin/resumen.texto: Army chief in the Six-Day War and prime minister who signed the Oslo Accords with Arafat (1993) and peace with Jordan (1994). He was assassinated by a Jewish extremist in 1995.

personas/peres/resumen.texto: Israeli politician who negotiated the Oslo Accords, for which he received the Nobel Peace Prize with Rabin and Arafat; he was prime minister and president.

personas/sharon/resumen.texto: Israeli general and politician, indirectly responsible, according to an Israeli commission, for the Sabra and Shatila massacre (1982). His visit to the Temple Mount in 2000 preceded the Second Intifada; as prime minister he withdrew Israel from Gaza in 2005.

personas/netanyahu/resumen.texto: The longest-serving prime minister in Israel’s history, who was in office when Hamas launched the October 7, 2023 attack and during the Gaza war.

personas/al-afgani/resumen.texto: Pan-Islamist activist who traveled the Muslim world calling for unity against European colonialism and for the reform of Islam. He replied to Renan that religion had held back science in Islam just as in Christianity.

personas/muhammad-abduh/resumen.texto: Disciple of al-Afghani and grand mufti of Egypt, father of Islamic modernism: Islam, he said, is compatible with modern reason and science.

personas/rashid-rida/resumen.texto: Syrian disciple of Abduh who, from his journal al-Manar in Cairo, moved from reformism to a more rigid Salafism and to opposition to Zionism; he influenced Hasan al-Banna.

personas/negib-azoury/resumen.texto: Lebanese Christian, former Ottoman official in Jerusalem, who in The Awakening of the Arab Nation (1905) predicted that Arab nationalism and Zionism would clash in Palestine.

personas/husein-ibn-ali/resumen.texto: Sharif of Mecca who, after his correspondence with the Briton McMahon, launched the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans in 1916. He proclaimed himself king of the Hejaz and was driven out by Ibn Saud.

personas/faisal-i/resumen.texto: Son of Sharif Hussein, leader of the Arab Revolt with T. E. Lawrence. He signed an agreement with Weizmann in 1919, was king of Syria in 1920 until France expelled him, and then king of Iraq.

personas/abdala-i/resumen.texto: Son of Sharif Hussein, emir of Transjordan and first king of Jordan, who annexed the West Bank. He was assassinated by a Palestinian at the al-Aqsa Mosque in 1951.

personas/lawrence/resumen.texto: British archaeologist and officer who accompanied the Arab Revolt; Seven Pillars of Wisdom narrates his experience and his sense that the Arabs had been betrayed.

personas/amin-al-husseini/resumen.texto: Grand mufti of Jerusalem appointed by the British and leader of Palestinian nationalism during the Mandate. During the Second World War he collaborated with Nazi Germany: he met Hitler in 1941, made radio propaganda for the Axis and helped recruit Balkan Muslims for the SS.

personas/izz-al-din-al-qassam/resumen.texto: Syrian preacher in Haifa who organized armed groups against the British and the Jewish settlers and died in combat in 1935. Hamas’s armed wing bears his name.

personas/hasan-al-banna/resumen.texto: Schoolteacher who founded the Muslim Brotherhood in 1928, the first mass Islamist movement, whose motto was “the Quran is our constitution.” Hamas was born in 1987 as its Palestinian branch.

personas/sayyid-qutb/resumen.texto: Ideologue of the Muslim Brotherhood, executed by Nasser. In Milestones (1964) he called on a vanguard to fight the societies he considered pagan, including Muslim ones; his essay Our Struggle with the Jews (c. 1950) presents the Jews as the eternal enemies of Islam.

personas/nasser/resumen.texto: President of Egypt and leader of pan-Arab nationalism, who nationalized the Suez Canal (1956) and was defeated by Israel in 1967.

personas/sadat/resumen.texto: President of Egypt who launched the 1973 war, traveled to Jerusalem in 1977 and signed peace with Israel in 1979. He was assassinated by Islamists of Egyptian Islamic Jihad in 1981.

personas/husein-de-jordania/resumen.texto: King of Jordan for almost half a century: he lost the West Bank in 1967, expelled the PLO in 1970 and signed peace with Israel in 1994.

personas/arafat/resumen.texto: Founder of Fatah and chairman of the PLO from 1969, a symbol of Palestinian nationalism. After decades of armed struggle, he recognized Israel and signed the Oslo Accords (1993); he presided over the Palestinian Authority until his death.

personas/ahmed-yassin/resumen.texto: Gaza cleric, quadriplegic since his youth, who founded Hamas in 1987 as a branch of the Muslim Brotherhood. He was killed in an Israeli strike in 2004.

personas/abdullah-azzam/resumen.texto: Palestinian from the West Bank, a Brotherhood theologian, who organized the Arab volunteers in Afghanistan. He argued that jihad in defense of any occupied Muslim land, from Afghanistan to Palestine, was the individual duty of every Muslim.

personas/bin-laden/resumen.texto: Saudi millionaire, disciple of Azzam, who founded al-Qaeda. In 1996 and 1998 he declared war on the United States and called for killing Americans and Jews; he ordered the September 11, 2001 attacks, which he claimed in 2004. He was killed in a US operation in Pakistan.

personas/jomeini/resumen.texto: Leader of the 1979 Iranian revolution and founder of the Islamic Republic, who made the struggle against Israel a state cause and instituted Jerusalem (al-Quds) Day.

personas/hasan-nasralah/resumen.texto: Secretary-general of Hezbollah from 1992 until Israel killed him in Beirut in September 2024.

personas/ismail-haniye/resumen.texto: Hamas prime minister after the 2006 elections and head of its political bureau; he was killed in an attack attributed to Israel in Tehran in July 2024.

personas/yahya-sinwar/resumen.texto: Leader of Hamas in Gaza and chief organizer of the October 7, 2023 attack; he was killed in combat with Israeli soldiers in Rafah in October 2024.

personas/mahmud-abbas/resumen.texto: Fatah leader who negotiated the Oslo Accords and has presided over the Palestinian Authority since 2005.

personas/edward-said/resumen.texto: Palestinian-American literary critic at Columbia University. In Orientalism (1978) he argued that European knowledge about the East was tied to colonial domination; he was also an advocate of the Palestinian cause and a critic of Oslo.

personas/mahmud-darwish/resumen.texto: The Palestinian national poet, who wrote the 1988 Palestinian Declaration of Independence.

personas/balfour/resumen.texto: British Foreign Secretary who in 1917 signed the letter in which his government supported “a national home for the Jewish people” in Palestine.

personas/lord-peel/resumen.texto: Former Secretary of State for India who chaired the 1936–1937 royal commission on Palestine, the first to propose partitioning it.

personas/benedicto-xvi/resumen.texto: German theologian and pope from 2005 to 2013. His Regensburg lecture (2006) on faith and reason, which quoted Manuel II on Muhammad, provoked protests in the Muslim world and later a dialogue with Muslim scholars.

personas/francisco-papa/resumen.texto: Argentine pope from 2013 to 2025, who signed the document on human fraternity (2019) with the grand imam of al-Azhar and called the Catholic parish in Gaza every night during the war.

personas/ahmed-al-tayeb/resumen.texto: Grand imam of al-Azhar, the most prestigious institution of Sunni Islam, and doctor of philosophy from the Sorbonne.

personas/bernard-lewis/resumen.texto: British-American historian of Islam and the Ottoman Empire. His essay “The Roots of Muslim Rage” (1990) coined the phrase “clash of civilizations”; Edward Said criticized him as an Orientalist.

personas/huntington/resumen.texto: Harvard political scientist whose The Clash of Civilizations (1996) argued that after the Cold War conflicts would be between civilizations, in particular between the West and Islam.

personas/runciman/resumen.texto: British historian of Byzantium whose A History of the Crusades (1951–1954) judged them a long act of intolerance in the name of God.

personas/amin-maalouf/resumen.texto: Lebanese writer in French, author of The Crusades Through Arab Eyes (1983) and In the Name of Identity (1998).

personas/yazid-ibn-abi-sufyan/resumen.texto: Commander of the Muslim conquest of Syria from 634, and the elder paternal half-brother of Muawiya. He led one of the four main columns at the Yarmouk (636) and, with Muawiya, took the ports of Sidon, Beirut and Byblos. When Abu Ubayda died in the plague of Amwas (639), the caliph Umar appointed him governor of Damascus, Jordan and Palestine, but he died of the same plague that year; Umar put Muawiya in his place in Damascus and Jordan.

personas/hasan-ibn-ali/resumen.texto: The eldest son of Ali and Fatima and grandson of Muhammad. After his father's murder he was recognized as caliph in Kufa (January 661), but Muawiya, governor of Syria, did not accept him; with his army demoralized by an assassination attempt and by desertions, he abdicated in August 661 in favor of Muawiya, on the condition, according to the sources, that he govern according to the Quran and the sunna, that the successor be chosen by a council (Muawiya broke this by designating Yazid I), and that his partisans be granted amnesty. Shiites count him as the second imam; among Sunnis, some count him as the fifth and last of the “rightly guided” caliphs. He died in Medina around 670 (50 AH; other sources give 49 AH and other years). The early sources, almost unanimously, say he was poisoned: according to most sources, by his wife Ja'da; Shiites and several early Sunni historians (al-Waqidi, al-Mada'ini, al-Baladhuri) name Muawiya as the instigator, accounts that al-Tabari omits; Veccia Vaglieri admits that he may have died of an illness.

personas/aisha/resumen.texto: Daughter of Abu Bakr and third wife of Muhammad. Sunni tradition counts her among the main transmitters of hadith (more than 2,000 are attributed to her) and among the teachers of the Prophet's companions; Shiites criticize her for having opposed Ali. In the First Fitna she led, with Talha and Zubayr, the opposition to Ali, who defeated them at the Battle of the Camel (December 656) and sent her back to Medina. Early sources say she was nine years old when the marriage was consummated, an age that is now debated and criticized.

personas/yibran-jalil-yibran/resumen.texto: Lebanese-American writer and painter, from a Maronite Christian family of Bsharri, in Ottoman Mount Lebanon; he emigrated to Boston in 1895. He studied in Beirut from 1898 to 1902, lived in Boston and, from 1911, in New York. He wrote in Arabic and in English; his best-known book, The Prophet (1923), was translated into more than a hundred languages. Some of his texts, with ideas of rebellion against Ottoman power and anticlerical views, were banned by the Ottoman authorities.

personas/abdala-bin-abdelaziz/resumen.texto: Tenth son of the founder of Saudi Arabia; crown prince from 1982 and de facto ruler from 1995, he was king from 2005 until his death. In 2002 he proposed the Arab Peace Initiative, which the Arab League adopted in Beirut: it offered normalization of relations with Israel in exchange for its withdrawal from the territories occupied in 1967, a Palestinian state with its capital in East Jerusalem, and an agreed solution for the refugees. Sharon's government rejected it for demanding a return to the 1967 borders, and Netanyahu expressed tentative support in 2015 and rejected it as a basis for negotiation in 2018.

personas/bashar-al-asad/resumen.texto: Son of Hafez al-Assad, whom he succeeded as president of Syria in 2000. His government repressed the protests of 2011, which turned into the Syrian civil war; the UN counted 306,887 civilians killed between 2011 and March 2021, and the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights gives more than 600,000 dead in total up to 2024. The OPCW and the joint UN–OPCW mechanism held his government responsible for chemical weapons attacks, such as the one at Khan Shaykhun in 2017; al-Assad called them “a 100% invention” and described the rebels as “terrorists”. He fled to Moscow on 8 December 2024, when rebels entered Damascus, and Russia granted him asylum.

personas/yazid-i/resumen.texto: Second Umayyad caliph, designated heir by his father Muawiya in the first case of hereditary succession to the caliphate. During his reign Husayn was killed at Karbala (680) by the troops of his governor of Kufa, Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad; his army sacked Medina after the battle of al-Harra (August 683) and besieged Mecca, where Ibn al-Zubayr had taken refuge; he died in November 683, and the Second Fitna began. For many Muslims he is an illegitimate ruler because of these events; modern historians judge him with more nuance and point out that he strengthened the defenses of Syria and did not conquer new territories.

personas/muawiya-ii/resumen.texto: Third Umayyad caliph and last of the Sufyanid branch, son of Yazid I. He reigned for a few months (sources give between twenty days and four months; most historians say no more than two), ill and with an authority limited to Damascus and southern Syria, while Ibn al-Zubayr was recognized as caliph in the Hijaz. He died without an heir, and the succession crisis passed power to the branch of Marwan I; the accounts of his reign, such as his abdication sermon, are considered partly sectarian or unreliable.

personas/marwan-i/resumen.texto: Cousin of the caliph Uthman, he was his secretary, governor of Medina and one of the Umayyad leaders in the Hijaz. After the death of Mu'awiya II he was elected caliph at Jabiya (684) and defeated at Marj Rahit (August 684) the Qays tribes that supported Ibn al-Zubayr; he again subdued Egypt, Palestine and northern Syria. He founded the Marwanid branch, which ruled until 750, and designated as his heir his son Abd al-Malik; he died in spring 685, perhaps of the plague then affecting Syria.

personas/abd-allah-ibn-al-zubayr/resumen.texto: Grandson of Abu Bakr and nephew of Aisha, he refused to recognize Yazid I, took refuge in Mecca and proclaimed himself caliph in 683. Almost all the provinces recognized him, but his authority was nominal outside the Hijaz; his brother Musab dominated Iraq until Abd al-Malik killed him in 691. Al-Hayyay ibn Yusuf besieged Mecca and killed him in October or November 692, ending the Second Fitna.

personas/suleiman-ibn-abd-al-malik/resum.texto: Seventh Umayyad caliph. As governor of Palestine he founded Ramla, which replaced Lod as the province's capital and remained so until the 11th century. As caliph (715–717) he dismissed the generals of the great expansion, such as the conqueror of Sind, and Musa ibn Nusayr; the expansion almost came to a halt, and his greatest undertaking, the siege of Constantinople (717–718), ended in an Arab defeat. He died at Dabiq during the siege.

personas/al-hadi/resumen.texto: Fourth Abbasid caliph, eldest son of al-Mahdi and brother of Harun al-Rashid. He reigned for a little over a year (785–786), amid power struggles with his mother, al-Jayzuran, and died in September 786; Harun succeeded him.

personas/al-amin/resumen.texto: Sixth Abbasid caliph, son of Harun al-Rashid and Zubayda, of Abbasid descent through both parents. When he tried to displace his half-brother al-Ma'mun from the succession, a civil war broke out; he was deposed and killed in Baghdad in September 813, and al-Ma'mun became caliph.

personas/al-mutasim/resumen.texto: Eighth Abbasid caliph, brother of al-Ma'mun. He formed a guard of Turkish mercenaries, founded Samarra as capital (836) and pursued the rationalist Mu'tazili policy of the mihna. He ordered the 838 campaign against the Byzantines that ended with the sack of Amorium.

personas/al-mustamsik/resumen.texto: Abbasid caliph of Cairo, under Mamluk tutelage: he reigned from 1497 to 1508, when he abdicated in favor of his son al-Mutawakkil III, and returned briefly in 1516, while the latter was a prisoner of the Ottomans, to invest the last Mamluk sultan, Tumanbay II. After the Ottoman conquest (1517) the Ottomans took his family's property and deported part of his family; he died in 1521. Other sources give other birth years (1447 and 1470).

personas/abdulmejid-ii/resumen.texto: Last Ottoman caliph. When the Grand National Assembly of Turkey abolished the sultanate (1 November 1922), the same assembly elected him caliph (19 November), without political power; the assembly also abolished the caliphate on 3 March 1924, and he went into exile. From Switzerland he argued that the abolition was contrary to sharia; he died in Paris in 1944 and was buried in Medina. Afterward, Hussein ibn Ali, sharif of Mecca, proclaimed himself caliph, with limited recognition.

personas/yigal-alon/resumen.texto: Palmach commander and general: in 1948 he led the conquest of Galilee, Lod and Ramla (from which between 50,000 and 70,000 Palestinians were expelled, under an order signed by his operations chief, Yitzhak Rabin, in Operation Dani, which Allon directed, according to Benny Morris) and of the Negev as far as Eilat. He served as minister and deputy prime minister, and as acting prime minister between the death of Eshkol and the election of Golda Meir in 1969. In 1967 he devised the Allon Plan, which proposed which territories to keep after the Six-Day War and which, though never officially adopted, guided Israeli settlement for a decade. He died of a heart attack in the middle of the campaign for the Labor leadership.

personas/ehud-olmert/resumen.texto: Mayor of Jerusalem (1993–2003) and prime minister of Israel from 2006 to 2009; he took over on an interim basis in January 2006, when Sharon was incapacitated by a stroke, and formed a government after the March elections. His government decided the 2006 Lebanon War, which the Winograd Commission criticized, ordered Operation Orchard (2007) and the Gaza war of 2008–2009. He negotiated with Abbas after the Annapolis conference (2007): they disagreed about the size of the land swap (Olmert asked for between 6.3% and 6.8% of the West Bank; Abbas, no more than 1.9%) and did not sign. According to Olmert's memoirs, Abbas hesitated; according to Bush's, Abbas broke off the negotiations when Olmert announced he was resigning. He resigned in 2008 because of corruption investigations; he was convicted in 2014 of bribery (the Holyland case) while he was mayor, and served prison time from 2016 to 2017.

personas/naftali-bennett/resumen.texto: Former commando and software entrepreneur, he led the religious Zionist party Jewish Home and later New Right and Yamina; he served as minister of economy, of education and of defense. After the 2021 elections he formed a rotating government with Yair Lapid: he was prime minister from 13 June 2021 to 30 June 2022, when the coalition failed to pass laws and the Knesset was dissolved. He opposes a Palestinian state and in 2013 proposed annexing Area C.

personas/yair-lapid/resumen.texto: Journalist and television presenter who founded the centrist party Yesh Atid (2012) and served as finance minister (2013–2014). In the 2021 rotating government he was foreign minister and, when the Knesset was dissolved, prime minister from 1 July to 29 December 2022 (181 days), until the government that emerged from the November elections was formed.

personas/hosni-mubarak/resumen.texto: Air force chief and vice president under Sadat, he succeeded him as president of Egypt in 1981 after his assassination and governed until 2011, with single-candidate referendums and a state of emergency almost always in force. He kept the peace with Israel and supported the Israeli–Palestinian peace process; his critics point to repression and corruption. He resigned after 18 days of protests in 2011; in 2012 he was sentenced to life imprisonment for failing to prevent the deaths of protesters (not for the deaths themselves), but the Court of Cassation annulled the sentence and acquitted him in 2017. In 2014 he was sentenced to three years for embezzlement; Cassation annulled that sentence and, in the new trial, he was sentenced again in 2015.

personas/sufi-abu-taleb/resumen.texto: Jurist, president of Cairo University and of the Egyptian parliament (1978–1983). After Sadat's assassination (6 October 1981) he served eight days as interim president, according to the Constitution, and handed the office to Vice President Mubarak.

personas/zakaria-mohieddin/resumen.texto: Egyptian officer, member of the Revolutionary Command Council of 1952, minister of the interior, vice president and prime minister (1965–1966). After the defeat of 1967, Nasser announced his resignation and named him as successor, a post he declined; Nasser stayed in office, so he never became president. In 1968 he gave up all his posts and left public life.

personas/talal-de-jordania/resumen.texto: King of Jordan after the assassination of his father, Abdullah I, in 1951, until Parliament forced him to abdicate in 1952 because of mental illness (schizophrenia, according to reports). His most remembered achievement is the 1952 constitution, which made the kingdom a constitutional monarchy. He spent the rest of his life in a sanatorium in Istanbul, and was succeeded by his son Hussein.

personas/abdala-ii-de-jordania/resumen.texto: King of Jordan since 7 February 1999, son of Hussein and Princess Muna; before that he was head of the special forces. A constitutional monarch with broad executive and legislative powers, which his critics consider an authoritarian regime, he responded to the protests of 2011 with changes of government and reforms, and kept the peace with Israel signed in 1994. He holds custody of the Muslim and Christian holy places of Jerusalem, which his dynasty has exercised since 1924.

personas/ahmed-qurei/resumen.texto: Born in Abu Dis, banker and Fatah leader, economic director of the PLO, he followed Arafat to Tunis and was one of the negotiators of the Oslo accords. He was president of the Palestinian Legislative Council and second prime minister of the Palestinian Authority, from 7 October 2003 until Fatah's electoral defeat in 2006 (interim until 29 March, when Haniyeh succeeded him); he also had charge of security.

personas/salam-fayyad/resumen.texto: Economist trained in the United States, finance minister of the Palestinian Authority and prime minister from June 2007 to June 2013. Abbas appointed him after Hamas took over Gaza, citing a “national emergency”; Hamas challenged it as illegal and went on recognizing Haniyeh in Gaza, and the Legislative Council never confirmed him. He is known for his economic reforms.

personas/rawhi-fattouh/resumen.texto: Fatah leader born in Rafah, president of the Palestinian Legislative Council since 2004. After Arafat's death (11 November 2004) he was interim president of the Palestinian Authority, according to the Basic Law, until Abbas won the elections and took office on 15 January 2005. In November 2024 Abbas designated him interim president in case of Abbas's death or resignation; in April 2025 he appointed Hussein al-Sheikh vice president.

personas/yahya-hammuda/resumen.texto: Lawyer born in Lifta, active in the cause of Palestinian refugees from 1949 (General Congress of Refugees). He chaired the PLO Executive Committee from 24 December 1967 to 2 February 1969, after the resignation of Ahmad Shukeiri and before Arafat took over the presidency; his tenure left no mark on the organization.

personas/roboam/resumen.texto: Son and successor of Solomon and last king of the united monarchy, according to the Hebrew Bible. Ten northern tribes rebelled around 932–931 BC and formed the kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam; Rehoboam became the first king of Judah. According to the books of Kings and Chronicles, in his fifth year Pharaoh Shishak invaded Judah and took fortified cities; extra-biblical evidence of his reign is scant.

personas/ali-zayn-al-abidin/resumen.texto: Fourth of the twelve Shiite imams, son of Husayn. He survived Karbala (680), was taken captive to Damascus and was allowed to return to Medina, where he lived in seclusion and took no part in the uprisings against the Umayyads; he is esteemed, even among the early Sunnis, as an authority in hadith and law. He died around 712, of natural causes or poisoned by the Umayyads, according to the sources, and was succeeded by his son Muhammad al-Baqir.

personas/aqsunqur-al-bursuqi/resumen.texto: Seljuk atabeg of Mosul in 1113–1114 and again from 1124, and shihna (military governor) of Iraq from 1120. On the sultan's orders he waged war against the Crusaders: in 1125 he took Aleppo for Sultan Mahmud II and supported Toghtekin at the battle of Azaz, where the Crusaders broke the siege. Ten Nizari assassins stabbed him to death in the Great Mosque of Mosul on 26 November 1126; he was succeeded by his son Masud.

hechos/llegada-de-los-filisteos/titulo.texto: The Philistines settle on the coast

hechos/llegada-de-los-filisteos/resumen.texto: One of the “Sea Peoples” who attacked Egypt in the time of Ramesses III settled on the southern coast of Canaan, in Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath. Through Greek, their name gave rise to that of Palestine.

hechos/reino-de-david-y-salomon/titulo.texto: The kingdom of David and Solomon

hechos/reino-de-david-y-salomon/resumen.texto: According to the Bible, David took Jerusalem from the Jebusites and made it the capital of a kingdom that united the tribes of Israel, and Solomon built the temple. Archaeology debates how large that kingdom was; the Tel Dan stele confirms a “House of David” a century and a half later.
