hechos/templo-de-salomon/resumen.texto: The temple attributed to Solomon housed the Ark of the Covenant and was the central sanctuary of the worship of Yahweh until the Babylonians destroyed it in 586 BC. No remains have been identified with certainty.

hechos/caida-de-samaria/resumen.texto: The Assyrians took Samaria after a three-year siege and deported part of its population; the kingdom of Israel disappeared and peoples brought from other provinces settled in the region. From this come the “ten lost tribes” of tradition.

hechos/campana-de-senaquerib/resumen.texto: The Assyrian king took Lachish and 46 other cities of Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage,” according to his annals; the Bible says an angel destroyed his army. Jerusalem did not fall and Judah paid tribute.

hechos/reforma-de-josias/resumen.texto: King Josiah centralized worship in the temple of Jerusalem and destroyed the sanctuaries of other gods, after the discovery of a “book of the law” that many scholars identify with Deuteronomy.

hechos/retorno-de-sion/resumen.texto: After conquering Babylon, Cyrus the Great allowed the deported Jews to return to Judah and rebuild the temple. The Bible calls him God’s “anointed.”

hechos/segundo-templo/resumen.texto: The returnees completed a modest temple under the governor Zerubbabel. It lasted almost six centuries, until AD 70, and gives its name to an entire era of Judaism.

hechos/sitio-de-tiro-332/resumen.texto: The Phoenician city, on an island, held out for seven months against Alexander the Great, who built a causeway to reach it. After its fall, Alexander passed through Gaza to Egypt and the region entered the Hellenistic world.

hechos/revuelta-macabea/resumen.texto: The priest Mattathias and his sons rose up against the ban on the Jewish religion decreed by Antiochus IV. Judas Maccabeus recovered and purified the temple in 164 BC, which Hanukkah celebrates; his brothers founded the Hasmonean kingdom.

hechos/conquista-de-pompeyo/resumen.texto: Called in by two Hasmonean brothers who were disputing the throne, Pompey took the Temple Mount and entered the Holy of Holies. Judea came under Roman tutelage.

hechos/templo-de-herodes/resumen.texto: Herod doubled the Temple esplanade with enormous retaining walls, of which the Western Wall is a section. It was one of the largest sanctuaries in the Roman world.

hechos/crucifixion-de-jesus/resumen.texto: The Roman prefect Pontius Pilate had Jesus of Nazareth crucified in Jerusalem during Passover, c. 30 or 33. His followers proclaimed his resurrection and, from Jerusalem, spread his message among Jews and Gentiles.

hechos/primera-guerra-judeo-romana/resum.texto: Judea's rebellion against Rome, divided among factions, ended with the siege of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Temple in 70. Josephus, a rebel commander who went over to the Romans, wrote its history.

hechos/academia-de-yavne/resumen.texto: After the destruction of the Temple, Yohanan ben Zakkai gathered the sages at Yavne. There rabbinic Judaism replaced sacrifices with prayer, study and the law.

hechos/sitio-de-masada/resumen.texto: The Tenth Legion besieged the fortress of the Sicarii and built a ramp to reach the wall. According to Josephus, the 960 defenders took their own lives before the Romans entered; Masada became a symbol of the State of Israel.

hechos/revuelta-de-bar-kojba/resumen.texto: The refounding of Jerusalem as a pagan colony sparked a new revolt, which Rome crushed with enormous losses. Judea was emptied of Jews, Jerusalem was barred to them and the province was renamed Syria Palaestina.

hechos/redaccion-de-la-misna/resumen.texto: Judah ha-Nasi set down the oral law in writing in six orders. It is the basis of the Talmud and of all later Jewish law.

hechos/construccion-del-santo-sepulcro/r.texto: Constantine ordered a temple of Venus demolished and the tomb identified as that of Jesus uncovered; a great basilica was built over it. From then on Jerusalem was the center of Christian pilgrimage.

hechos/templo-de-juliano/titulo.texto: Julian attempts to rebuild the Temple

hechos/templo-de-juliano/resumen.texto: The pagan emperor ordered the Jewish Temple rebuilt, but work stopped because of a fire, perhaps caused by an earthquake, and Julian died soon after in Persia. Christian authors saw it as a miracle.

hechos/revueltas-samaritanas/resumen.texto: The Samaritans rebelled several times against the Christian Empire, which persecuted them; after the revolt of 529 Justinian repressed them harshly and their numbers fell for good.

hechos/conquista-persa-de-jerusalen/resu.texto: The army of Khosrow II, with the support of Jews from Galilee, took Jerusalem after a siege; thousands of Christians died, churches burned and the True Cross was carried off to Persia.

hechos/restitucion-de-la-vera-cruz/resum.texto: After defeating Persia, Heraclius entered Jerusalem with the relic of the Cross. The victory was short-lived: four years later the Arabs arrived.

hechos/primera-revelacion/resumen.texto: According to Islamic tradition, the angel Gabriel appeared to Muhammad in a cave on Mount Hira and dictated to him the first verses of the Quran: “Read, in the name of your Lord!”

hechos/hegira/resumen.texto: Persecuted in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers emigrated to Yathrib, which came to be called Medina. There the first Muslim political community was born; the caliph Umar fixed that year as the first of the Islamic calendar.

hechos/batalla-de-badr/resumen.texto: About 300 Muslims from Medina defeated a Meccan army three times larger that was protecting a caravan. The Quran presents it as a victory granted by God.

hechos/batalla-de-uhud/resumen.texto: The Meccans, with Khalid ibn al-Walid commanding the cavalry, defeated the Muslims near Medina; Muhammad was wounded.

hechos/batalla-de-la-trinchera/resumen.texto: A coalition of Mecca and allied tribes besieged Medina but could not cross the ditch the Muslims had dug; the siege failed.

hechos/banu-qurayza/resumen.texto: After the siege, Muhammad besieged the Jewish tribe of the Banu Qurayza, accused of having negotiated with the besiegers. According to Ibn Ishaq, their men, between 600 and 900, were beheaded and the women and children enslaved; the other two Jewish tribes, the Qaynuqa and the Nadir, had earlier been expelled from Medina. Some historians dispute the figures.

hechos/batalla-de-jaibar/resumen.texto: The Muslims conquered the Jewish oasis of Khaybar, whose inhabitants were allowed to keep farming it in exchange for half the harvest. It became a model for the later treatment of subject Jews and Christians.

hechos/tratado-de-hudaybiyya/resumen.texto: Ten-year truce between Muhammad and Mecca, which allowed the Muslims to make the pilgrimage the following year.

hechos/batalla-de-mutah/resumen.texto: First clash between the Muslims and the Byzantines and their Arab allies, east of the Dead Sea; the Muslims withdrew after losing their three commanders.

hechos/conquista-de-la-meca/resumen.texto: Muhammad entered Mecca almost without fighting, destroyed the idols of the Kaaba and granted amnesty to most of his former enemies.

hechos/expedicion-de-tabuk/resumen.texto: Muhammad led a large army toward the Byzantine frontier without meeting battle and obtained the submission of Jewish and Christian communities in the north in exchange for tribute, as provided for in sura 9 of the Quran.

hechos/muerte-de-mahoma/resumen.texto: Muhammad died in Medina without designating an undisputed successor. The Companions chose Abu Bakr as caliph; the partisans of Ali held that the office belonged to him.

hechos/guerras-de-la-ridda/resumen.texto: Many tribes stopped paying tribute to Medina after Muhammad's death, and other prophets arose. Abu Bakr subdued them and unified all of Arabia for the first time, which then launched itself against Syria and Iraq.

hechos/batalla-de-yarmuk/resumen.texto: The Arabs under Khalid and Abu Ubayda destroyed the army of Heraclius by the Yarmouk River. According to tradition, the emperor bade farewell to Syria: “Farewell, Syria, my beautiful province.”

hechos/batalla-de-qadisiyya/resumen.texto: The Arabs defeated the Sasanian army near the Euphrates and took its capital, Ctesiphon. Persia fell completely in the following years.

hechos/sitio-de-jerusalen-637/resumen.texto: After a siege, the patriarch Sophronius surrendered the city to the caliph Umar, who according to tradition came in person to receive it. The Christians kept their churches in exchange for tribute, and the Jews were allowed to live in the city again.

hechos/recension-del-coran/titulo.texto: Uthman establishes the text of the Quran

hechos/recension-del-coran/resumen.texto: The caliph Uthman had an official text of the Quran copied and sent to the provincial capitals, and the divergent versions burned. The oldest surviving manuscripts date from that period or slightly earlier.

hechos/conquista-del-magreb/resumen.texto: The conquest of North Africa took sixty years because of Byzantine and, above all, Berber resistance, with Kusaila and the Kahina. Once converted to Islam, the Berbers formed the bulk of the army that crossed into Hispania in 711.

hechos/batalla-de-karbala/resumen.texto: Husayn, grandson of Muhammad, died with some seventy followers facing the army of the Umayyad caliph Yazid. The event sealed the division between Sunnis and Shiites.

hechos/sitio-de-constantinopla-674/resum.texto: Muawiya's fleet blockaded Constantinople for several summers in a row. Greek fire, an incendiary liquid invented by a Syrian refugee, destroyed part of its ships and the caliph sued for peace.

hechos/cupula-de-la-roca-hecho/titulo.texto: Construction of the Dome of the Rock

hechos/cupula-de-la-roca-hecho/resumen.texto: Abd al-Malik built on the Temple Mount a shrine that rivaled the Christian churches in splendor. Its inscriptions quote the Quran on Jesus: “the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is only the messenger of God”; say not “three”.

hechos/caida-de-cartago-698/resumen.texto: Hassan ibn al-Nu'man took and razed the capital of Byzantine Africa, which a Byzantine fleet had briefly recovered. Tunis replaced it as the main city.

hechos/sitio-de-constantinopla-717/resum.texto: A huge Umayyad army and fleet besieged the city for a year. Leo III held out with Greek fire and the help of the Bulgars; hunger and winter decimated the besiegers. Many historians consider it decisive for the history of Europe.

hechos/revolucion-abasi/resumen.texto: A revolt that began in Khorasan overthrew the Umayyads; almost their entire family was murdered. A survivor, Abd al-Rahman, founded the Emirate of Córdoba. The capital of the caliphate moved from Damascus to Iraq.

hechos/fundacion-de-bagdad/resumen.texto: The caliph al-Mansur founded a round city on the Tigris. Baghdad was the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and of the great translation movement from Greek into Arabic.

hechos/conquista-de-sicilia/resumen.texto: The Aghlabids of Ifriqiya took 75 years to wrest Sicily from Byzantium. The island remained Muslim until the Norman conquest of 1061-1091.

hechos/saqueo-de-roma-846/resumen.texto: A Muslim fleet sailed up the Tiber and sacked the basilicas of St. Peter and St. Paul, outside the walls. Pope Leo IV later surrounded the Vatican with the Leonine Wall.

hechos/recuperacion-de-antioquia-969/res.texto: The generals of Nikephoros II took Antioch, which remained Byzantine until 1084. It was the high point of the Byzantine reconquest in the East.

hechos/fatimies-en-palestina/resumen.texto: After conquering Egypt in 969, the Ismaili caliphs of Cairo occupied Palestine and southern Syria, which they contested for a century with Bedouins, Byzantines and Turks.

hechos/destruccion-del-santo-sepulcro/ti.texto: Al-Hakim orders the destruction of the Holy Sepulchre

hechos/destruccion-del-santo-sepulcro/re.texto: The Fatimid caliph ordered the church demolished as part of a persecution of Christians and Jews. The news reached Europe and, in the long run, fed the idea of the crusade; the church was partly rebuilt from 1027 under an agreement with Byzantium.

hechos/toma-de-jerusalen-1073/resumen.texto: A Turkoman chief, Atsiz, took Jerusalem from the Fatimids; in 1077 he crushed a revolt with a massacre. Christian pilgrims told Europe of the hardships of the journey under the Turks.

hechos/concilio-de-piacenza/titulo.texto: Byzantium asks for help at Piacenza

hechos/concilio-de-piacenza/resumen.texto: In March 1095, envoys of Alexios I Komnenos came to Urban II's council and asked for help against the Turks who were occupying Anatolia, according to the chronicler Bernold of Constance. Eight months later, at Clermont, the pope turned that request into an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

hechos/cruzada-popular/resumen.texto: Tens of thousands of peasants and poor knights followed Peter the Hermit to Constantinople. Alexios I ferried them over to Asia, where the Turks annihilated them at Civetot.

hechos/masacres-de-renania/titulo.texto: Massacres of Jews on the Rhine

hechos/masacres-de-renania/resumen.texto: Bands of crusaders, above all that of Count Emicho, attacked the Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms, Mainz and Cologne, despite the protection of some bishops. Thousands died or took their own lives rather than accept baptism; the Hebrew chronicles remember them as martyrs.

hechos/sitio-de-antioquia-1098/resumen.texto: After an eight-month siege, an act of treachery opened Antioch to the crusaders, who were in turn besieged by the atabeg Kerbogha. The discovery of the “Holy Lance” restored their morale and they won.

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital/titulo.texto: Recognition of the Order of the Hospital

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital/resumen.texto: Pope Paschal II recognized the confraternity that ran the pilgrims' hospital of St. John in Jerusalem. The Hospitallers became a military order and continued on Rhodes and Malta.

hechos/batalla-de-ager-sanguinis/titulo.texto: Battle of the Field of Blood

hechos/batalla-de-ager-sanguinis/resumen.texto: The emir Ilghazi of Mardin annihilated the army of Antioch; its prince, Roger of Salerno, died in the battle.

hechos/fundacion-del-temple/resumen.texto: Hugh de Payens and other knights swore to protect pilgrims and received lodging from King Baldwin II in the al-Aqsa Mosque, the “Temple of Solomon”. Bernard of Clairvaux gave them a theological justification: the warrior monk.

hechos/caida-de-edesa/resumen.texto: The fall of the first crusader state shook the West and prompted the Second Crusade. In the Muslim world, Zengi was hailed as a champion of jihad.

hechos/segunda-cruzada-damasco/titulo.texto: The Second Crusade fails before Damascus

hechos/segunda-cruzada-damasco/resumen.texto: Kings Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany attacked Damascus, which had been an ally of Jerusalem, and withdrew after four days. The failure pushed Damascus toward Nur al-Din.

hechos/fin-de-los-fatimies/resumen.texto: Sent to Egypt by Nur al-Din, Saladin became vizier and abolished the Shiite caliphate of Cairo, returning Egypt to Sunnism. With Egypt and then Syria, he encircled the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

hechos/batalla-de-montgisard/resumen.texto: The young leper king Baldwin IV, with the Templars, surprised and defeated Saladin's army near Ramla.

hechos/reconquista-de-jerusalen-1187/res.texto: After Hattin, Saladin besieged Jerusalem, defended by Balian of Ibelin, who surrendered it on 2 October. Unlike in 1099 there was no massacre: the Christians paid ransom, many of the poor were enslaved, the cross on the Dome of the Rock was torn down and Saladin invited the Jews to return.

hechos/sitio-de-acre-1189/resumen.texto: One of the longest sieges of the Middle Ages: the crusaders besieged Acre while Saladin besieged them. The arrival of Richard and Philip Augustus brought about its surrender.

hechos/matanza-de-ayyadieh/resumen.texto: Richard the Lionheart had some 2,700 Muslim prisoners from Acre executed in sight of Saladin's camp when the agreed exchange was delayed.

hechos/batalla-de-arsuf/resumen.texto: Richard defeated Saladin on the coastal plain and took Jaffa, but did not attack Jerusalem.

hechos/tratado-de-jaffa-1192/resumen.texto: Three-year truce between Richard and Saladin: the crusaders kept the coast from Tyre to Jaffa, and Christian pilgrims could visit Jerusalem unarmed.

hechos/reino-de-chipre/resumen.texto: Richard had taken Cyprus in 1191 from a Byzantine usurper; after he sold it to the Templars, the island passed to Guy of Lusignan, whose family reigned until 1489.

hechos/quinta-cruzada/resumen.texto: The crusaders attacked Egypt, took Damietta and rejected al-Kamil's offer to exchange it for Jerusalem. They marched on Cairo and were trapped by the Nile flood.

hechos/francisco-y-al-kamil/titulo.texto: Francis of Assisi before the sultan

hechos/francisco-y-al-kamil/resumen.texto: In the midst of the Fifth Crusade, Francis crossed the lines to preach before the sultan al-Kamil, who received him and let him return. Over the centuries the meeting became a symbol of dialogue between Christianity and Islam.

hechos/tratado-de-jaffa-1229/titulo.texto: Frederick II recovers Jerusalem by treaty

hechos/tratado-de-jaffa-1229/resumen.texto: The excommunicated emperor Frederick II negotiated with al-Kamil the handover of Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Nazareth for ten years, leaving the Temple Mount to the Muslims. He was criticized by both the pope and the ulama.

hechos/saqueo-de-jerusalen-1244/resumen.texto: Khwarazmian mercenaries allied with the sultan of Egypt took and sacked the city. Jerusalem did not return to Christian hands until 1917.

hechos/batalla-de-la-forbie/resumen.texto: Near Gaza, the Khwarazmians and Baybars destroyed the last great army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, allied with the princes of Damascus and Homs.

hechos/batalla-de-mansura/resumen.texto: The Seventh Crusade was destroyed in the Nile Delta and the king of France was taken prisoner. In the midst of the crisis, the Mamluks seized power in Egypt.

hechos/saqueo-de-bagdad/resumen.texto: Hulagu's army took Baghdad, killed the last Abbasid caliph and tens of thousands of inhabitants, and destroyed its libraries. It was experienced as the end of an era of Islam.

hechos/batalla-de-ain-yalut/resumen.texto: The Mamluks of Qutuz and Baybars defeated the Mongols in Galilee, the first great Mongol defeat, and saved Egypt.

hechos/caida-de-antioquia-1268/resumen.texto: Baybars took Antioch, killed or enslaved its inhabitants and wrote the absent prince a mocking letter describing the destruction. The city never recovered.

hechos/caida-de-acre-1291/resumen.texto: The sultan al-Ashraf Khalil took Acre after a six-week siege; Tyre, Sidon and Atlit were evacuated. It was the end of the crusader states in the Holy Land; the young Abulfeda took part in the siege.

hechos/custodia-de-tierra-santa/titulo.texto: The Franciscans take custody of the holy places

hechos/custodia-de-tierra-santa/resumen.texto: Following an agreement between the kings of Naples and the Mamluk sultan, the pope entrusted the Franciscans with the custody of the Latin shrines, which they retain to this day.

hechos/saqueo-de-damasco-1401/resumen.texto: The Turco-Mongol conqueror took Damascus, sacked it and set fire to the Umayyad Mosque. Ibn Khaldun, who was in the city, met with him.

hechos/batalla-de-marj-dabiq/resumen.texto: Selim I destroyed the Mamluk army north of Aleppo. Syria, Palestine and, the following year, Egypt became Ottoman for four centuries.

hechos/sitio-de-rodas-1522/resumen.texto: After a six-month siege, the Hospitallers surrendered Rhodes and left with honors; Charles V gave them Malta in 1530.

hechos/sitio-de-viena-1529/resumen.texto: Suleiman besieged Vienna after conquering Hungary and withdrew when winter came. For two centuries the Turkish advance was the great threat to Central Europe and a theme of the Reformation.

hechos/murallas-de-jerusalen/titulo.texto: Suleiman rebuilds the walls of Jerusalem

hechos/murallas-de-jerusalen/resumen.texto: The sultan surrounded the city with the walls and gates that today mark the bounds of the Old City.

hechos/gran-sitio-de-malta/resumen.texto: The Hospitallers under Grand Master La Valette held out for four months against a large Ottoman fleet until reinforcements arrived from Sicily.

hechos/caida-de-famagusta/resumen.texto: The Ottomans took Nicosia and, after a siege of almost a year, Famagusta; its Venetian commander, Bragadin, was flayed alive despite the agreed surrender.

hechos/batalla-de-lepanto/resumen.texto: The fleet of the Holy League (Spain, Venice, the Papacy and others) destroyed the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras. Cervantes lost the use of his left hand there; Europe celebrated it as the salvation of Christendom, although the Ottomans rebuilt their fleet within a year.

hechos/proclamacion-de-sabetai-zevi/resu.texto: The prophet Nathan of Gaza proclaimed Sabbatai Zevi the messiah. The news shook the Jewish communities of Europe and the East, which sold their possessions to go to the Holy Land; his conversion to Islam in 1666 was a lasting trauma.

hechos/batalla-de-viena-1683/resumen.texto: An Imperial and Polish army, with King John III Sobieski, broke the second Ottoman siege of Vienna. From then on the Ottomans retreated in Europe.

hechos/statu-quo/titulo.texto: The Status Quo of the holy places

hechos/statu-quo/resumen.texto: A decree of the sultan fixed the division of the shrines of Jerusalem and Bethlehem among the Orthodox, Latins, Armenians and other Churches, confirmed in 1852. The dispute over these rights was one of the pretexts for the Crimean War.

hechos/sitio-de-acre-1799/resumen.texto: After conquering Egypt, Napoleon invaded Palestine and besieged Acre, defended by Ahmad al-Jazzar with British help. Plague and failure forced him to return to Egypt.

hechos/ocupacion-egipcia-de-siria/titulo.texto: Ibrahim Pasha rules Syria and Palestine

hechos/ocupacion-egipcia-de-siria/resume.texto: The son of Muhammad Ali, governor of Egypt, conquered Syria and Palestine and opened the region to European consuls, missionaries and merchants. The powers forced him to return it to the sultan.

hechos/conflicto-de-1860/titulo.texto: Massacres of Christians in Lebanon and Damascus

hechos/conflicto-de-1860/resumen.texto: A war between Druze and Maronites in Mount Lebanon ended in massacres of thousands of Christians, which spread to the Christian quarter of Damascus. The Algerian emir Abd el-Kader saved many by sheltering them in his house; France sent troops.

hechos/primera-aliya/resumen.texto: After the Russian pogroms of 1881, some 25,000 Jews from Eastern Europe and Yemen emigrated to Palestine and founded agricultural colonies such as Rishon LeZion and Zikhron Ya'akov, many of them supported by Baron Edmond de Rothschild.

hechos/congreso-sionista-de-basilea/resu.texto: Herzl gathered delegates from all over the world in Basel, who founded the Zionist Organization and approved the goal of “a home for the Jewish people in Palestine secured by public law”.

hechos/yihad-otomana-1914/resumen.texto: On entering the First World War, the sultan-caliph proclaimed jihad against Britain, France and Russia and called on the Muslims of their colonies to rebel. The call found little echo, and the British responded by supporting the revolt of the Sharif of Mecca.

hechos/genocidio-armenio/resumen.texto: The Young Turk government deported the Armenians of Anatolia to the deserts of Syria; between 600,000 and more than a million died in marches, massacres and camps such as Deir ez-Zor. Assyrians and Greeks of the Empire were also massacred.

hechos/revuelta-arabe/resumen.texto: Sharif Hussein of Mecca rose against the Ottomans on British promises of an independent Arab kingdom. His sons Faisal and Abdullah, with T. E. Lawrence, reached Damascus in 1918.

hechos/declaracion-balfour-hecho/resumen.texto: The British government declared that it viewed “with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people”, without prejudice to the civil and religious rights of the “non-Jewish communities”, who made up 90% of the population.

hechos/batalla-de-jerusalen-1917/resumen.texto: General Allenby entered Jerusalem on foot on 11 December 1917, ending four centuries of Ottoman rule. The European press presented it as the end of a crusade.

hechos/conferencia-de-san-remo/resumen.texto: The Allied powers allocated the mandates over the Arab provinces of the Ottoman Empire: Syria and Lebanon to France; Palestine and Iraq to Britain, with the Balfour Declaration incorporated into the mandate.

hechos/disturbios-de-1920/resumen.texto: During the Muslim festival of Nebi Musa, Arab crowds attacked the Jewish quarter of Jerusalem; five Jews and four Arabs were killed. It was the first major violence of the Mandate and led to the creation of the Haganah.

hechos/matanza-de-hebron/resumen.texto: Amid riots over the use of the Western Wall, Arabs of Hebron killed 67 Jews of the city's ancient community; many Arab families hid and saved Jewish neighbors. The British evacuated the survivors.

hechos/revuelta-arabe-1936/resumen.texto: A general strike and then an Arab armed uprising against the Mandate and Jewish immigration, suppressed by the British with thousands of deaths. There were also attacks on Jews and reprisals by the Irgun.

hechos/comision-peel/resumen.texto: The British royal commission concluded that the Mandate was unworkable and proposed dividing Palestine into a Jewish state, an Arab state united with Transjordan and a British zone including Jerusalem. The Arabs rejected it; the Zionist Congress accepted it as a basis for negotiation.

hechos/husseini-y-hitler/titulo.texto: The Mufti of Jerusalem meets Hitler

hechos/husseini-y-hitler/resumen.texto: Amin al-Husseini, a refugee in Berlin, asked Hitler for support for Arab independence and against the Jewish national home; Hitler told him that Germany sought the destruction of the Jewish element in the East as well. The mufti collaborated with the Nazi regime until 1945.

hechos/farhud/resumen.texto: After the fall of a pro-German government, crowds attacked the Jews of Baghdad for two days; some 180 were killed. It was the beginning of the end of a 2,600-year-old community.

hechos/holocausto/resumen.texto: Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered some six million European Jews. The catastrophe made the creation of a Jewish state urgent for Zionism and for much of the world.

hechos/atentado-hotel-rey-david/resumen.texto: The Irgun, Begin's Zionist armed organization, blew up the wing of the hotel housing the British administration; 91 people were killed, Arabs, British and Jews.

hechos/descubrimiento-de-los-manuscritos.texto: Discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls
Bedouin shepherds found jars containing scrolls in a cave near the Dead Sea. By 1956 some 900 manuscripts had turned up in eleven caves, the oldest known biblical texts.

hechos/plan-de-particion/titulo.texto: The UN votes to partition Palestine

hechos/plan-de-particion/resumen.texto: The General Assembly approved, by 33 votes to 13, dividing Palestine into a Jewish state and an Arab state, with Jerusalem under an international regime. The Jewish Agency accepted it; the Palestinian Arab leaders and the Arab states rejected it.

hechos/guerra-civil-1947/resumen.texto: The day after the vote, fighting broke out between Jewish and Arab militias, with bombings, ambushes and sieges such as that of Jerusalem. From April 1948 the Haganah went on the offensive and the mass exodus of the Arab population began.

hechos/matanza-de-deir-yassin/resumen.texto: Irgun and Lehi fighters attacked the Arab village of Deir Yassin, near Jerusalem, and killed some 110 inhabitants, including women and children. The news accelerated the flight of the Palestinians.

hechos/convoy-de-hadassah/resumen.texto: Arab forces attacked a convoy of doctors, nurses and patients heading to the Hadassah hospital on Mount Scopus and killed 78 people, in retaliation for Deir Yassin.

hechos/independencia-de-israel/resumen.texto: On 14 May 1948, hours before the end of the Mandate, Ben-Gurion read out in Tel Aviv the declaration of the State of Israel, which promised equal rights to all its inhabitants “irrespective of religion, race or sex”.

hechos/guerra-de-1948/resumen.texto: Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq invaded the territory of the Mandate. Israel held out and ended up with more territory than under the partition plan; Jordan took the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and Egypt took Gaza.

hechos/nakba/resumen.texto: About 700,000 Arab Palestinians, more than half of the total (711,000 according to the UN Conciliation Commission in 1949), fled or were expelled from their homes during the 1947-1949 war, and Israel did not allow them to return; between 400 and 600 villages were destroyed. The causes are debated: Benny Morris concludes that in the first stage they left mainly because of Jewish attacks or fear of them, and that there were direct expulsions afterward (Lod and Ramla, July 1948); Ilan Pappé sees in Plan Dalet a plan of expulsion; Efraim Karsh maintains that there was no Jewish design and that in Haifa many left at Arab urging, something Walid Khalidi denies. Palestinians call it the Nakba, “the catastrophe.”

hechos/exodo-judio-de-paises-arabes/titu.texto: Jewish exodus from the Arab countries and Iran

hechos/exodo-judio-de-paises-arabes/resu.texto: Between 800,000 and one million Jews left the Arab and Muslim countries, from Morocco to Iraq and Yemen, amid persecution, expropriation and the pull of the new state; most settled in Israel.

hechos/armisticios-de-1949/resumen.texto: Israel signed armistices with Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria. The ceasefire lines, the “Green Line”, were the de facto border until 1967.

hechos/crisis-de-suez/resumen.texto: After Nasser nationalized the canal, Israel invaded the Sinai in agreement with Britain and France, which landed at Port Said. The United States and the USSR forced them to withdraw.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-olp/resumen.texto: The Arab League created the Palestine Liberation Organization in East Jerusalem. From 1969 it was led by Arafat, of Fatah, and became the recognized representative of the Palestinians.

hechos/guerra-de-los-seis-dias/resumen.texto: Faced with the Egyptian mobilization and the closure of the Straits of Tiran, Israel struck first and in six days occupied the Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. For the first time since 1948, Jews were able to pray at the Western Wall.

hechos/cumbre-de-jartum/resumen.texto: The Arab League responded to the defeat with “the three noes”: no peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with it.

hechos/septiembre-negro/resumen.texto: King Hussein forcibly expelled from Jordan the Palestinian armed organizations, which had formed a state within the state; they settled in Lebanon.

hechos/masacre-de-munich/resumen.texto: The Palestinian group Black September, linked to Fatah, took Israeli athletes hostage at the Munich Olympic Games; eleven Israelis were killed.

hechos/guerra-de-yom-kipur/resumen.texto: Egypt and Syria launched a surprise attack on the holiest day of Judaism. Israel recovered and counterattacked, but the war opened Sadat's path toward peace and triggered the Arab oil embargo.

hechos/matanza-de-maalot/resumen.texto: Militants of the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine seized a school in Ma'alot, in Galilee; 25 hostages, 22 of them children, were killed during the Israeli assault.

hechos/matanza-de-la-carretera-costera/l.texto: Coastal Road, north of Tel Aviv

hechos/matanza-de-la-carretera-costera/r.texto: A Fatah commando that arrived by sea hijacked a bus on the coastal road; 38 Israeli civilians were killed, 13 of them children. Israel responded by invading southern Lebanon.

hechos/acuerdos-de-camp-david-hecho/resu.texto: Sadat and Begin, with Jimmy Carter, agreed on the return of the Sinai in exchange for peace and on a framework for Palestinian autonomy that was never implemented. Sadat had earlier traveled to Jerusalem and addressed the Knesset (1977).

hechos/paz-egipto-israel/resumen.texto: Egypt was the first Arab country to recognize Israel; it recovered the Sinai in 1982 and was expelled from the Arab League for a time.

hechos/revolucion-irani/resumen.texto: The revolution led by Khomeini created a Shiite Islamic republic that made the struggle against Israel a cause of state and backed Hezbollah, Hamas and Islamic Jihad.

hechos/asesinato-de-sadat/resumen.texto: Members of Egyptian Islamic Jihad killed Sadat during a military parade, as punishment for the peace with Israel. Ayman al-Zawahiri, later head of al-Qaeda, was imprisoned after the attack.

hechos/guerra-del-libano-1982/resumen.texto: Israel invaded Lebanon to drive out the PLO and besieged Beirut; Arafat and his fighters left for Tunis. The Israeli occupation of the south lasted until 2000.

hechos/matanza-de-sabra-y-chatila/resume.texto: Lebanese Christian Phalange militiamen killed hundreds or thousands of Palestinian and Lebanese civilians in two Beirut refugee camps surrounded by the Israeli army. An Israeli commission found the defense minister, Ariel Sharon, indirectly responsible.

hechos/atentados-de-beirut-1983/resumen.texto: Two suicide truck bombs killed 241 American and 58 French servicemen of the multinational force. They were claimed by the Islamic Jihad Organization, regarded as a front for Hezbollah, which presented itself publicly in 1985.

hechos/primera-intifada/resumen.texto: A popular Palestinian uprising in Gaza and the West Bank, with strikes, boycotts and stones thrown at the Israeli army. More than a thousand Palestinians and some 160 Israelis were killed; it led to the Oslo negotiations.

hechos/fundacion-de-hamas/resumen.texto: At the start of the intifada, Sheikh Ahmed Yassin and other leaders of the Muslim Brotherhood in Gaza founded the Islamic Resistance Movement, Hamas. Its 1988 charter called for the destruction of Israel through jihad.

hechos/declaracion-de-independencia-pale.texto: The Palestinian National Council, meeting in Algiers, proclaimed the State of Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, on the basis of Resolution 181, which implied accepting the existence of Israel.

hechos/conferencia-de-madrid/resumen.texto: The first direct negotiation between Israel, Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and the Palestinians, organized by the United States and the USSR after the Gulf War.

hechos/atentado-embajada-de-israel/titul.texto: Israeli embassy bombing in Buenos Aires

hechos/atentado-embajada-de-israel/lugar.texto: Embassy of Israel in Buenos Aires

hechos/atentado-embajada-de-israel/resum.texto: A car bomb destroyed the Israeli embassy; 29 people were killed. It was claimed by the Islamic Jihad Organization, linked to Hezbollah, and the Argentine Supreme Court attributed it to Hezbollah.

hechos/acuerdos-de-oslo-hecho/resumen.texto: Israel and the PLO recognized each other and signed in Washington, with the handshake between Rabin and Arafat, a declaration of principles negotiated in secret in Oslo: a transitional Palestinian autonomy and a final agreement within five years, which never came. Hamas rejected it.

hechos/matanza-de-la-cueva-de-los-patria.texto: Baruch Goldstein, a far-right Israeli settler, killed 29 Muslims praying in the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron. Hamas responded with its first suicide bombings inside Israel.

hechos/atentado-de-la-amia/resumen.texto: A car bomb destroyed the headquarters of the Jewish mutual aid association AMIA in Buenos Aires; 85 people were killed, the deadliest attack in Argentine history. The Argentine courts attributed it to Hezbollah acting on orders from the government of Iran; in 2024 a court classified the attack as a crime against humanity.

hechos/paz-israel-jordania/resumen.texto: Rabin and King Hussein signed the peace at the Wadi Araba border; Jordan was the second Arab country to recognize Israel.

hechos/atentado-autobus-dizengoff/resume.texto: A Hamas suicide bomber killed 22 people on a bus on Dizengoff Street; the organization claimed the attack.

hechos/asesinato-de-rabin/resumen.texto: Yigal Amir, a Jewish extremist opposed to the Oslo Accords, killed the prime minister at the end of a peace rally in Tel Aviv.

hechos/cumbre-de-camp-david-2000/resumen.texto: Bill Clinton brought together Ehud Barak and Arafat for a final agreement; it failed, mainly over Jerusalem and the refugees, and each side blamed the other.

hechos/segunda-intifada/resumen.texto: After Sharon's visit to the Temple Mount, a new and far more armed Palestinian uprising, with waves of suicide bombings by Hamas, Islamic Jihad and Fatah's al-Aqsa Brigades, and harsh Israeli military operations. Some 3,000 Palestinians and 1,000 Israelis were killed.

hechos/atentado-de-sbarro/resumen.texto: A suicide bomber killed 15 civilians, seven of them children, in a pizzeria in central Jerusalem. Hamas and Islamic Jihad claimed it; the woman who guided the attacker, Ahlam Tamimi, was released in 2011 in a prisoner exchange.

hechos/atentados-11-s/resumen.texto: Nineteen members of al-Qaeda hijacked four airplanes and crashed them into the Twin Towers, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania; nearly 3,000 people were killed. Bin Laden at first denied involvement and claimed responsibility in a 2004 video.

hechos/matanza-de-pesaj/resumen.texto: A Hamas suicide bomber entered the Passover dinner at the Park Hotel in Netanya and killed 30 people, most of them elderly. Israel responded with Operation Defensive Shield in the West Bank.

hechos/operacion-escudo-defensivo/resume.texto: The Israeli army reoccupied the cities of the West Bank; the battle of Jenin and the siege of Arafat's Mukataa were its hardest episodes.

hechos/barrera-de-cisjordania/titulo.texto: Construction of the West Bank barrier

hechos/barrera-de-cisjordania/resumen.texto: Israel began building a wall and fence to stop the attacks; much of it runs inside the West Bank, and the International Court of Justice declared it illegal in those sections in 2004.

hechos/atentados-de-madrid-2004/resumen.texto: Bombs on four commuter trains killed 193 people. They were carried out by a jihadist cell inspired by al-Qaeda, which claimed them in a video as punishment for Spain's participation in the Iraq War.

hechos/retirada-de-gaza/resumen.texto: Sharon's government evacuated the 21 Jewish settlements in Gaza and four in the northern West Bank, but kept control of the Strip's borders, airspace and sea.

hechos/atentados-de-londres-2005/resumen.texto: Four British suicide bombers killed 52 people on the Underground and a bus. Two of them left recorded videos justifying the attack; al-Qaeda released them.

hechos/elecciones-palestinas-2006/resume.texto: Hamas won a majority in the Palestinian Legislative Council; Israel, the United States and the European Union demanded that it recognize Israel and renounce violence, and cut off aid to the new government.

hechos/toma-de-gaza-por-hamas/resumen.texto: After months of clashes, Hamas drove Fatah out of Gaza. Since then it has governed the Strip, which is under an Israeli and Egyptian blockade, while the Palestinian Authority governs part of the West Bank.

hechos/guerra-de-gaza-2008/resumen.texto: To stop Hamas rockets, Israel bombed and invaded the Strip; some 1,400 Palestinians and 13 Israelis were killed.

hechos/guerra-de-gaza-2014/resumen.texto: After the kidnapping and murder of three Israeli teenagers and of a Palestinian teenager in retaliation, seven weeks of rockets and bombing left more than 2,000 Palestinians and 73 Israelis dead.

hechos/califato-del-estado-islamico/titu.texto: The Islamic State proclaims a caliphate

hechos/califato-del-estado-islamico/resu.texto: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi proclaimed himself caliph in the al-Nuri Mosque in Mosul. The Islamic State persecuted Yazidis, Christians and Shiites, destroyed monuments such as those of Palmyra and claimed attacks in Europe with videos and statements.

hechos/atentados-de-enero-de-2015/resume.texto: Two brothers linked to al-Qaeda in Yemen killed twelve people at the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo over its cartoons of Muhammad; a third terrorist, who declared himself a member of the Islamic State, killed a policewoman and four Jews in a kosher supermarket.

hechos/atentados-de-paris-2015/resumen.texto: Islamic State commandos killed 130 people at the Bataclan concert hall, in bars and outside the Stade de France. The Islamic State claimed them in a statement.

hechos/acuerdos-de-abraham/resumen.texto: The United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, and later Morocco and Sudan, established relations with Israel through United States mediation, without a prior agreement with the Palestinians.

hechos/ataque-del-7-de-octubre/resumen.texto: Thousands of fighters from Hamas and other Gaza groups crossed the border and attacked kibbutzim, towns, military bases and a music festival at Re'im; they killed some 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and took 251 hostages. It was the day with the most Jews killed since the Holocaust.

hechos/guerra-de-gaza-2023/resumen.texto: Israel responded to October 7 with an air and ground campaign to destroy Hamas and recover the hostages. Tens of thousands of Palestinians were killed according to the Gaza Health Ministry, controlled by Hamas, and most of the Strip was destroyed and its population displaced, with famine; South Africa accused Israel of genocide before the International Court of Justice. A ceasefire in October 2025 allowed the release of the living hostages.

hechos/caida-de-asad/resumen.texto: A rebel offensive led by the Islamist group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham took Damascus in December 2024 and ended more than half a century of rule by the Assad family.

hechos/traduccion-latina-del-coran/titul.texto: First Latin translation of the Quran

hechos/traduccion-latina-del-coran/resum.texto: Commissioned by Peter the Venerable, Robert of Ketton translated the Quran into Latin. The abbot of Cluny wanted to know Islam in order to refute it by reason; the translation, a paraphrase, was read in Europe until the 18th century.

hechos/conferencia-de-ratisbona/resumen.texto: Benedict XVI spoke at his former university on faith and reason and quoted Manuel II, who asked a Muslim to show him what new thing Muhammad had brought, “and you will find only evil and inhuman things, such as his command to spread the faith by the sword”. There were protests and attacks on churches; a year later 138 Muslim scholars responded with “A Common Word”.

hechos/batalla-de-hunain/resumen.texto: Shortly after the capture of Mecca, Muhammad, with some 12,000 men, faced the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes in the valley of Hunayn, on the road to Taif. According to Muslim tradition, the army initially fell into disarray under an ambush and regrouped around Muhammad; the battle ended in a Muslim victory and a large booty. It is one of the few battles named in the Quran (sura 9).

hechos/batalla-de-adjnadayn/resumen.texto: The first major pitched battle between the Byzantine army and that of the Rashidun Caliphate, in July or August 634 near Beit Guvrin; it ended in a Muslim victory and left the interior of Palestine open, whose cities surrendered almost without resistance. It is known mainly from Muslim sources, such as al-Waqidi (9th century), as there is no contemporary Byzantine account; the army sizes these sources give are considered greatly exaggerated (Gibb supposes about 10,000 men per side; Morray, about 20,000).

hechos/sitio-de-damasco-634/resumen.texto: The Muslims besieged Damascus from August 21 to September 19, 634; it was the first major Byzantine city to fall in the conquest of Syria (other sources put the fall in 635 or 637). The accounts combine two versions: Khalid ibn al-Walid entered by assault through the eastern gate while Thomas, commander of the garrison, negotiated the surrender with Abu Ubayda at the Jabiya Gate; the commanders then discussed the terms, and Abu Ubayda's terms were accepted.

hechos/batalla-de-los-mastiles/resumen.texto: A naval engagement off the coast of Lycia, near present-day Finike, between the fleet of Emperor Constans II and that of the caliphate, commanded by Abu al-A'war, admiral of Muawiya. According to al-Tabari, the Arabs won, with heavy losses on both sides, and Constans escaped with difficulty (Theophanes recounts that he did so by swapping his clothes with those of an officer). Sebeos adds that the fleet continued to Constantinople and that a storm sank its siege engines; the Arab sources do not mention this.

hechos/batalla-de-akroinon/resumen.texto: One of the three columns of the largest Umayyad expedition in decades, some 20,000 men, was confronted near Akroinon (today Afyon), in Phrygia, by Emperor Leo III and his son Constantine V. Theophanes recounts that the two Arab commanders fell, along with some 13,200 men, and that the rest withdrew in good order. It was a Byzantine victory which, combined with the instability of the caliphate, the traditional reading saw as decisive in ending the great Arab raids into Anatolia for about three decades; Brooks, Kaegi and Lilie attribute that end to the caliphate's defeats on other fronts and to its internal wars.

hechos/saqueo-de-amorio/resumen.texto: The Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim, in retaliation for the previous year's expedition by Theophilus, defeated the Byzantine forces at Anzen and reached Amorium, cradle of the reigning dynasty, on August 1, 838. An inhabitant revealed a weak point in the walls; the commander of the sector secretly negotiated with the caliph and abandoned his post, and the city was taken and destroyed: many inhabitants were killed and the rest taken off as slaves, and the captive dignitaries were executed years later at Samarra. For the Byzantines it was a trauma, and it discredited the iconoclasm that Theophilus upheld, which was abandoned shortly after his death (842).

hechos/batalla-de-harran/resumen.texto: On May 7, 1104, the Seljuks of Jikirmish (Mosul) and Sökmen (Mardin) defeated, after a feigned retreat, the Crusaders of Antioch and Edessa led by Bohemond, Tancred and Baldwin of Edessa; Baldwin and Joscelin were captured. It was the first major defeat of the Crusader states: Antioch lost territory to Aleppo and Byzantium, and Bohemond returned to Italy to recruit troops. William of Tyre wrote that no battle had been more disastrous. The exact location is debated: most historians accept Albert of Aachen and Fulcher, who place it across from Raqqa, two days from Harran (the point on the map is approximate); Ibn al-Athir places it 12 km from Harran.

hechos/batalla-de-marj-ayyun/resumen.texto: In June 1179, near the Litani River, Baldwin IV of Jerusalem, with the Templars and Raymond III of Tripoli, defeated a raiding party of Saladin's and, believing the battle won, was attacked by the main Ayyubid army and defeated. The king, ill with leprosy and no longer able to mount a horse, escaped capture thanks to his guard; the Templar Grand Master Odo of Saint-Amand was taken prisoner. William of Tyre blamed the Templars for their recklessness; the order, however, did not answer to the king. In August Saladin destroyed the castle of Jacob's Ford.

hechos/batalla-de-jafa-1192/resumen.texto: After Richard I sailed north, Saladin took Jaffa at the end of July 1192, except for the citadel. Richard arrived by sea with a small force (fifty-four knights, a few hundred infantrymen and some 2,000 Genoese and Pisan crossbowmen), recovered the city, and on August 5 repulsed Saladin's counterattack with a line of lancers and crossbowmen. It was the last combat of the Third Crusade: shortly afterward the Truce of Jaffa was signed, leaving the Crusaders the strip from Tyre to Jaffa (Beirut was taken in 1197).

hechos/cruzada-de-los-barones/resumen.texto: An expedition called by Pope Gregory IX, led first by Theobald I of Navarre (who arrived in Acre on September 1, 1239) and then by Richard of Cornwall (October 1240 to May 1241). A group that set out without permission was defeated near Gaza on November 13, 1239, and in December an Ayyubid emir took Jerusalem. Afterward Theobald took advantage of the war between the Ayyubids of Damascus and Egypt to negotiate with both sides, and the kingdom recovered Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Nazareth and much of Galilee. Assessments differ: recent historiography judges it the most successful territorial venture since the First Crusade; other works call it a failure with no lasting results. The gains were lost in 1244.

hechos/guerra-de-kitos/titulo.texto: Jewish Revolt in the Diaspora (Kitos War)

hechos/guerra-de-kitos/resumen.texto: During Trajan's campaign against the Parthians, Jewish communities in Egypt, Cyrenaica and Cyprus rose up almost at the same time, and there was resistance in Mesopotamia. According to Cassius Dio and Eusebius, the rebels attacked above all their neighbors, with extreme violence; Marcius Turbo suppressed the revolts with harsh reprisals that destroyed or annihilated Jewish communities. The sources are scarce and late (Dio writes a century later, Eusebius two centuries later). The name “Kitos War” comes from Lusius Quietus, who put down the revolt in Mesopotamia and was later governor of Judea; today it is debated whether there was a separate uprising there. Thirteen years later Hadrian refounded Jerusalem as a Roman colony, and the Bar Kokhba revolt broke out.

hechos/disturbios-de-jaffa-1921/resumen.texto: From May 1 to 7, 1921, there were riots that began as a clash between two Jewish May Day parades, that of the Communist Party and that of Ahdut HaAvoda, and became attacks by Arabs on Jews (in an immigrant hostel and in Abu Kabir, where the writer Yosef Haim Brenner died), and then reprisals by Jews against Arabs. Forty-seven Jews and 48 Arabs were killed, the latter mostly by fire from the police and British troops. The Haycraft Commission concluded that the underlying cause was Arab hostility toward Jews, for political and economic reasons tied to Jewish immigration and Zionist policy; the report displeased both sides.

hechos/disturbios-de-1929/resumen.texto: From August 23 to 29, after a dispute over access to and ritual objects at the Western Wall (the Buraq, for Muslims), Arabs attacked Jews in Jerusalem, Hebron and Safed, destroying Jewish property. The Shaw Commission records that in some cases Jews attacked Arabs, almost always in reprisal (the family of Imam Abd al-Ghani Awn in Jaffa, the Nebi Akasha mosque). A total of 133 Jews and 116 Arabs were killed (the latter mostly by the police and British troops; some 20 at the hands of Jews or from indiscriminate British fire), and 339 Jews and at least 232 Arabs were wounded. The worst violence was in Hebron and Safed, and in Hebron hundreds of Jews were saved by Arab neighbors who hid them. The Shaw Commission attributed the underlying cause to Arab opposition to the political consequences of Zionism and to economic fears, and the trigger to the Jewish demonstration at the Wall on August 15; many historians point to the agitation of Mufti Amin al-Husseini over an alleged threat to the Temple Mount, and others (Pappé, Kreiner) to Arab frustration at the lack of representative institutions. 174 Arabs and 109 Jews were charged with murder or attempted murder, and about 40% of the Arabs and 3% of the Jews were convicted.

hechos/guerra-de-desgaste/resumen.texto: Fighting between Israel and Egypt, with Jordan, the PLO and their allies, after the Six-Day War. With the Arab policy of the “three noes” (no peace, no recognition, no negotiation) and Nasser convinced that only force would achieve the withdrawal from Sinai, the artillery duels over the Suez Canal became, from March 8, 1969, massive bombardments, air war and commando raids. It ended in August 1970 with a ceasefire under the Rogers Plan, with no change of borders. Israel bombed inside Egypt (January to April 1970), including the attack on the Bahr el-Baqar school (April 8, 1970, 46 pupils killed). Israeli dead were about 921 according to Ze'ev Schiff and a little over 600 according to Chaim Herzog; Egyptian dead were 2,882 according to Saad el-Shazly and about 10,000 soldiers and civilians according to Benny Morris. Israel accused Egypt and the Soviets of moving missiles forward toward the canal.

hechos/operacion-entebbe/resumen.texto: On June 27, 1976, members of the PFLP-External Operations and the German Revolutionary Cells hijacked an Air France flight from Tel Aviv to Paris and took it to Entebbe, Uganda; they demanded the release of 53 prisoners. According to witnesses, Ugandan soldiers guarded the hostages together with the hijackers, opened the wall that had separated the Israelis, and then fired on the commandos. On the night of July 3-4, Israeli commandos, after flying more than 4,000 km, rescued 102 of the 106 remaining hostages, killed all the hijackers and about 45 Ugandan soldiers. Three hostages died, as did the unit's commander, Yonatan Netanyahu. Dora Bloch, who was in a hospital in Kampala, was later murdered by the Ugandan authorities. Because of Kenya's help to Israel, Amin had about 245 Kenyans killed.

hechos/operacion-litani/titulo.texto: 1978 Israeli Invasion of Southern Lebanon (Operation Litani)

hechos/operacion-litani/resumen.texto: On March 14, 1978, Israel invaded southern Lebanon as far as the Litani River, three days after the Coastal Road massacre, in which Fatah militants who had come from Lebanon killed 38 Israeli civilians. Between 1,100 and 2,000 Lebanese and Palestinians were killed, along with about 20 Israelis, and between 100,000 and 250,000 people were displaced within Lebanon. The PLO withdrew north; the Security Council, in Resolutions 425 and 426, called for Israeli withdrawal and created UNIFIL. Israel withdrew in 1978, handing the border strip over to the militia of Saad Haddad (the future South Lebanon Army), not to UNIFIL.

hechos/guerra-de-gaza-2012/resumen.texto: From November 14 to 21, 2012, Israel attacked the Gaza Strip; it began with an airstrike that killed Ahmed Yabari, Hamas's military chief in Gaza. Israel said it was responding to more than a hundred rockets within 24 hours and to other attacks; the Palestinians blamed Israel for the earlier escalation and pointed to the blockade and the occupation. 174 Palestinians were killed according to the UN Human Rights Council (2013), 107 of them civilians; according to B'Tselem there were 167, of whom 62 took part in the fighting, and according to the Israeli army 177, of whom 120 were combatants. Hamas and Islamic Jihad fired more than 1,450 rockets, which killed six Israelis: four civilians and two soldiers. An Egyptian-mediated ceasefire ended the fighting; both sides claimed victory, and Human Rights Watch said both had violated the laws of war.

hechos/muerte-de-muhammad-al-durrah/resu.texto: On September 30, 2000, the second day of the Second Intifada, Muhammad al-Durrah, aged 12, died at the Netzarim junction in Gaza, in a shootout between the Israeli army and Palestinian forces. A Palestinian cameraman for France 2 filmed the father and son, and correspondent Charles Enderlin attributed the shots to Israeli positions. The boy was proclaimed a martyr in the Muslim world. There was no criminal investigation and no full autopsy. Who fired remains disputed: the Israeli army initially assumed responsibility and later withdrew it; the investigation commissioned by the Israeli army in 2000 (Nahum Shahaf) considered it “quite plausible” that he was hit by Palestinian bullets; the Palestinian conclusion, by General Abdel-Razek al-Majaydeh, was that the bullets came from the Israeli post; the Israeli report of 2013 (the Kuperwasser commission, which did not interview the father, the cameraman or Enderlin) concluded that he had not been hit by Israeli fire and that perhaps he had not even been wounded, something the father rejected and Enderlin and France 2 criticized. In 2013 a French court convicted Philippe Karsenty of defamation; he had claimed the scene had been staged.

hechos/primera-fitna/resumen.texto: First civil war of the Muslim community, beginning with the assassination of Caliph Uthman (656). Ali, the fourth caliph, defeated Aisha, Talha and Zubayr at the Battle of the Camel (December 656), and in 657 faced Muawiya, governor of Syria, who demanded revenge for Uthman, at Siffin; the arbitration that followed led the Kharijites to break away from Ali, who defeated them at Nahrawan. A Kharijite assassinated Ali in 661; his son Hasan ceded power to Muawiya, and the Umayyad caliphate began. Shiites see Ali as the rightful successor of the Prophet; Sunni tradition counts him as the fourth of the first four caliphs.

hechos/batalla-de-siffin/resumen.texto: In July 657, on the banks of the Euphrates near Raqqa, Caliph Ali and Muawiya, governor of Syria, clashed. When Ali's Iraqis began to gain the upper hand, the Syrians raised Qur'ans on their lances, asking that the Book of God decide, and Ali accepted arbitration under pressure from most of his troops. The arbitration ended without result in 658, confirmed Muawiya and weakened Ali. According to Nasr ibn Muzahim, each army had about 150,000 men—or 100,000 for Ali's and 130,000 for Muawiya's—and the accounts speak of tens of thousands of dead; the figures cannot be verified.

hechos/sitio-de-nicea-1097/resumen.texto: The first major operation of the First Crusade, from 14 May to 19 June 1097. Nicaea, capital of the Seljuk sultanate of Rum since the Turks took it from Byzantium in 1081, had its sultan, Kilij Arslan, far away, at war with the Danishmendids; the Crusaders defeated him on 21 May when he returned. When Alexios I sent boats overland to Lake Ascania, the garrison negotiated and surrendered to the Byzantines on 19 June, before the Crusaders could assault the city; the Crusaders, who were not allowed to plunder it, were resentful of Byzantium.

hechos/batalla-de-dorilea-1097/resumen.texto: On 1 July 1097, near present-day Eskişehir, Kilij Arslan surprised the Crusader vanguard of Bohemond of Taranto, which was about five kilometers from the main body. Modern estimates give about 10,000 men to Bohemond and 6,000 or 7,000 horsemen to Kilij Arslan; Raymond of Aguilers speaks of 150,000 Turks and Fulcher of Chartres of 360,000, figures that historians reject. Reinforcements under Godfrey, Raymond and others arrived in time, the Turks fled leaving their camp, and the victory opened the way through Anatolia. Albert of Aachen gives 4,000 Crusaders and 3,000 Turks dead.

hechos/batalla-de-ascalon-1099/resumen.texto: On 12 August 1099, a few weeks after taking Jerusalem, the army of Godfrey of Bouillon (about 10,200 men, according to Raymond of Aguilers) surprised the camp of the Fatimid vizier al-Afdal (about 20,000, a modern estimate; the Gesta Francorum gives 200,000), asleep before the walls of Ascalon, and defeated it in less than an hour. Ibn al-Qalanisi estimates 12,700 Fatimid dead; the Crusaders killed those who surrendered. Godfrey did not take Ascalon, because its garrison wanted to surrender only to Raymond of Toulouse, and the city remained a Fatimid base until 1153.

hechos/sitio-de-jerusalen-1099/resumen.texto: From 7 June to 15 July 1099 the Crusaders besieged Jerusalem, held by the Fatimids for only a few months. After a failed assault on 13 June, with siege towers built from timber brought from near Nablus and with the help of English and Genoese sailors, they entered on 15 July. Christian, Muslim and Jewish chronicles agree that there was a slaughter of Muslims and Jews, including women and children. Raymond of Aguilers wrote that in Solomon's Porch men rode in blood up to their knees and bridles; Albert of Aachen describes a second massacre days later, of those who had been spared in exchange for ransom; Ibn al-Qalanisi reports that the Jews gathered in their synagogue and the Franks burned it over them, although a letter from the Cairo Geniza confirms the fire without mentioning people inside, and other Geniza letters document Jews who were ransomed. There are no reliable figures: Ibn al-Athir gives 70,000 dead, which does not fit a population of about 30,000, and modern estimates range from 3,000 to 10,000. Godfrey of Bouillon took the title “Defender of the Holy Sepulchre”.

hechos/primera-cruzada/resumen.texto: Armed expedition that Urban II called at the Council of Clermont (1095), after the appeal for help from Alexios I Komnenos at Piacenza, to bring Jerusalem back into Christian hands. First set out the People's Crusade of Peter the Hermit, annihilated at Civetot (October 1096); the massacres of Jews in the Rhineland (Speyer, Worms, Mainz) were carried out mainly by the bands of Count Emicho, which dispersed in Hungary. Then came the princes' crusade (Raymond of Toulouse, Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond, Robert of Normandy and others, who according to modern estimates numbered between 60,000 and 100,000 people including non-combatants). They took Nicaea (1097), won at Dorylaeum, took Antioch (1098) and Jerusalem (15 July 1099), defeated the Fatimids at Ascalon, and founded the Latin states of Edessa, Antioch and Jerusalem.

hechos/cuarta-cruzada/resumen.texto: Called by Innocent III to recover Jerusalem, a goal its leaders planned to reach by first attacking Ayyubid Egypt, it ended with the capture of Constantinople. The Crusaders could not pay the fleet they had contracted from Venice, and Doge Enrico Dandolo led them to sack Zara, a Christian city (November 1202), for which the pope temporarily excommunicated them. In 1203 they agreed to restore in Constantinople Isaac II and his son Alexios, who promised help for the Holy Land; after Alexios was overthrown in January 1204, the Crusaders took and sacked the city in April 1204, and only a few went on to the Holy Land. The Byzantine Empire was divided and the Latins founded an empire of their own. Historians debate whether the diversion was a consequence of the debts to Venice or had been planned earlier.

hechos/guerras-arabo-bizantinas/resumen.texto: Series of wars between the caliphates and the Byzantine Empire, beginning with the Muslim conquests and lasting until the 11th century (some authors extend them to the mid-12th century). After Yarmouk, the Muslims took Syria, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa within a few decades; the two sieges of Constantinople (674–678 and 717–718) failed, and the frontier was fixed at the Taurus mountains. Vassals of the Abbasids conquered Crete (827) and Sicily (from 831); between 920 and 976 the Byzantines recovered ground in Anatolia and northern Syria, and the Fatimids checked their advance. After 1071 the Seljuks took much of Anatolia.

hechos/conquista-musulmana-de-persia/res.texto: The Rashidun Caliphate conquered the Sasanian Empire, worn down by the war with Byzantium (602–628) and by a civil war after the death of Khosrow II. The first invasion (633) took part of Mesopotamia; after the victory at Qadisiyya (636) the Sasanians lost everything west of present-day Iran, and from 642 Umar ordered a full invasion; by 651 nearly all the country's cities were in Muslim hands, except the Caspian provinces and Transoxiana. Arab sources show that many localities resisted the invaders.

hechos/conquista-arabe-de-armenia/resume.texto: Campaigns of the Rashidun Caliphate against Byzantine Armenia. The first raids were in 639–640, there was an Arab defeat in 642, and in 652 the Armenian prince Theodore Rshtuni, an ally of Byzantium, broke with the Byzantines, made a pact with Muawiya, then governor of Syria, and accepted Muslim rule. After his death (654) and the Arab internal wars from 656 that control weakened, and it was reaffirmed when Muawiya became caliph in 661. The details are uncertain, because the Arab, Greek and Armenian sources contradict one another; the main ones are Bishop Sebeos, the priest Lewond and, above all, al-Baladhuri.

hechos/conquista-omeya-de-hispania/resum.texto: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the strait in 711, under the orders of Musa ibn Nusayr, governor of Ifriqiya, with a force of a few thousand men (the sources give between 1,700 and 7,000), and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic at Guadalete in July; Musa arrived later. Theodemir of Murcia surrendered on terms in 713; around 717 there were raids into Septimania, and in 719 Barcelona and Narbonne fell. The Arab forces were joined by Berbers converted after the conquest of the Maghreb. According to tradition, the defeat of an Umayyad army by Pelagius at Covadonga left a Christian stronghold in the north.

hechos/califato-abasi/resumen.texto: Third Islamic caliphate, of the dynasty descended from al-Abbas, uncle of Muhammad, which overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and ruled from Iraq until 1258; from 762 its capital was Baghdad, which became a center of science and culture with the House of Wisdom. Its height is associated with Harun al-Rashid (786–809). After a civil war an army of Turkish slaves was created and a new capital was built at Samarra (836); the provinces gained autonomy and, in the 10th century, the caliphs became figureheads under the Buyids, who took Baghdad in 945, and the Seljuks, who took it in 1055. It ended with the sack of Baghdad by Hulagu's Mongols and the execution of al-Musta'sim in 1258. A nominal Abbasid caliphate continued in Cairo (1261–1517), under Mamluk tutelage, until al-Mutawakkil III; see al-Mustamsik.

hechos/sayfo/resumen.texto: Massacres and deportations of Assyrian and Syriac Christians from south-eastern Anatolia and Persian Azerbaijan by Ottoman forces and some Kurdish tribes during World War I (“sayfo” means “sword” in Syriac). They began in August 1914, when Assyrian villages near the border were burned, and continued during the Ottoman occupation of Azerbaijan (January to May 1915); in Hakkari the Assyrian tribes resisted until they were expelled in September, and the governor Mehmed Reshid led the massacre of the Christians of the province of Diyarbekir. The Assyrian-Chaldean delegation estimated 250,000 dead at the Paris conference of 1919 (about half the population) and 275,000 at Lausanne (1923); neither figure can be confirmed. It was contemporary with the Armenian genocide and is linked to it; historians give local actors more weight than in the Armenian case, although the government also ordered attacks. Among the motives identified by historiography are the alleged disloyalty of Assyrian communities and the seizure of their lands. Several countries recognize it as genocide, and the government of Turkey rejects that designation.

hechos/incidente-de-la-gran-mezquita/tit.texto: Seizure of the Grand Mosque in Mecca

hechos/incidente-de-la-gran-mezquita/res.texto: From 20 November to 4 December 1979, up to 600 men led by Juhayman al-Utaybi, a Saudi Islamist opposed to the monarchy, seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, took hostages and proclaimed Muhammad al-Qahtani, Juhayman's brother-in-law, as the Mahdi; they denounced the House of Saud's alliance with the West and secularism. Saudi forces, with French GIGN advisers, retook the site after two weeks of fighting; 255 people died during the seizure according to the official Saudi figure (others give 270). Those captured, among them Juhayman, were sentenced to death: 63 were beheaded in public on 9 January 1980 in eight cities (other accounts give 68). Khomeini accused the United States and Israel, which set off anti-American riots in several countries; King Khalid gave more power to the ulama and the religious police.

hechos/conflicto-israeli-palestino/resum.texto: Dispute between Israelis and Palestinians over the territory of the former British Mandate of Palestine, which remains open: the borders and status of the West Bank, Gaza and Jerusalem, Israeli settlements, Palestinian refugees and their claim to return (resolution 194), and Israel's security and mutual recognition. Palestinians trace it to Zionism and Jewish immigration under the Mandate, and to their expulsion or flight in 1948 (the Nakba); Israel and the Zionists attribute it to the Arab rejection of the 1947 partition plan and to violence against Jews, and maintain that its 1948 war was defensive. Since 1967 Israel has occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem (which it annexed) and Gaza; it withdrew settlers and soldiers from Gaza in 2005 and has blockaded it since 2007. The International Court of Justice opined in 2004 that the wall and the settlements violate international law, and in 2024 that Israel's continued presence in the whole occupied Palestinian territory, Gaza included, is unlawful and must end. Israel rejected both opinions, holds that the West Bank is disputed territory, and says it has not occupied Gaza since 2005. The Oslo negotiations, Camp David (2000) and Annapolis did not reach a final agreement.

hechos/guerra-civil-libanesa/resumen.texto: Multi-sided war that caused about 120,000 deaths and displaced almost a million people, according to estimates. It broke out on 13 April 1975 in Beirut: gunmen fired on a church in Ayn al-Rummaneh and killed four people, among them two Maronite Phalangists, and hours later the Phalangists killed about 30 Palestinians who were traveling on a bus. It pitted Christian militias against the PLO and its Lebanese Muslim, leftist and Pan-Arabist allies, over sectarian tensions in the confessional system and the armed Palestinian presence. In January 1976 Maronite militias killed between 1,000 and 1,500 people in Karantina, and Palestinian militias retaliated at Damur. Syria intervened from 1976 (12,000 soldiers in June), and its troops stayed until 2005; Israel invaded in 1978 and 1982, and there were international peacekeeping forces. The Taif Agreements (1989) laid the foundations for the end of the war; the militias were disbanded in 1990, and a general amnesty followed in 1991. Hezbollah kept its weapons, which it justifies by resistance to the Israeli occupation of the south.

hechos/operacion-opera/resumen.texto: On 7 June 1981, Israeli F-16 fighters, escorted by F-15s, surprise-bombed the unfinished Iraqi nuclear reactor at Osirak, 17 km southeast of Baghdad; ten Iraqi soldiers and a French civilian were killed. Iraq and France, which had sold the reactor in 1976, said it was for peaceful research. Israel saw it as a source of nuclear weapons and presented the attack as self-defense (“it had less than a month left before it began operating”); the government declared that it was “a precedent for any future Israeli government” (the “Begin Doctrine”). The Security Council condemned the attack unanimously on 19 June (resolution 487), and international criticism, including that of the United States, was harsh; the attack came three weeks before the Israeli elections. Richard Betts, Malfrid Braut-Hegghammer and the Duelfer Report argue that the attack accelerated or set off Iraq's secret nuclear program.

hechos/operacion-pata-de-palo/resumen.texto: On 1 October 1985 Israeli aircraft bombed the PLO headquarters at Hammam Chott, near Tunis, about 2,060 km away: Israel's farthest action since Entebbe (1976). Between 41 and 71 people died, depending on the source: Israel spoke of about 60 PLO members; hospital sources, of 47. Israel presented it as a response to the murder of three Israelis on a yacht in Larnaca (Cyprus) on 25 September, which it attributed to the PLO's Force 17 (the PLO denied this), and which was itself a response to the capture of four commanders of that force by the Israeli navy on 9 September. The Security Council condemned the attack on 4 October as a violation of the UN Charter (resolution 573), with the abstention of the United States.

hechos/conflicto-del-sur-del-libano/resu.texto: After withdrawing from the rest of Lebanon in 1985, Israel kept a “security zone” in the south, with about 1,500 of its own soldiers and 2,500 of the South Lebanon Army, the allied Christian militia. Hezbollah, which arose from the occupation and was backed by Iran and Syria, waged guerrilla war and fired rockets into Galilee. Israel carried out Operation Accountability (1993) and Operation Grapes of Wrath (1996), in which more than 150 Lebanese civilians died, most of them in the Israeli shelling of the UN base at Qana. At the Jiam detention center of the South Lebanon Army, prisoners were tortured. After a helicopter accident in 1997, the Four Mothers movement demanded a withdrawal; Israel completed it in May 2000, and the South Lebanon Army collapsed with it.

hechos/conflicto-israeli-libanes/resumen.texto: After Israel's withdrawal in 2000, Hezbollah continued with intermittent attacks on the border, citing Israeli control of the Shebaa Farms, until the 2006 war; after that there was relative calm, with violations on both sides (Israeli overflights of Lebanon; Hezbollah not disarming, as Resolution 1701 required). From 8 October 2023 Hezbollah fired rockets and artillery at Israeli positions in the Shebaa Farms, in support of Hamas in the Gaza war, and Israel responded; about 96,000 people were displaced in Israel and more than 1.4 million in Lebanon. In September 2024 Hezbollah's pagers and radios exploded in an attack attributed to Israel, and Hassan Nasrallah was killed in an Israeli strike in Beirut (27 September). On 1 October an Israeli invasion of southern Lebanon began, which ended with a ceasefire on 27 November. The Lebanese Ministry of Health counted 3,583 dead in Lebanon from mid-September to mid-November 2024 and said most were civilians; Hezbollah's leader, Naim Qassem, said 5,000 of its fighters had died. In April 2025 Hezbollah said it was willing to discuss its disarmament with President Joseph Aoun if Israel withdrew from five positions in the south and halted its attacks. Fighting resumed on 2 March 2026, after the war of the United States and Israel against Iran, and there were truces in April and June.

hechos/guerra-del-libano-2006/resumen.texto: 34-day war between Hezbollah and Israel, from 12 July to 14 August (the Israeli blockade was lifted on 8 September). It began when Hezbollah fired diversionary rockets at Shlomi and other towns, ambushed Israeli soldiers at the border, killed three and captured two; five others died in the rescue attempt (eight in total). Israel responded with air and artillery strikes on military targets and Lebanese civilian infrastructure, including Beirut airport, with a blockade and a ground invasion; Hezbollah fired about 4,000 rockets at northern Israel, according to Israeli sources. Between 1,191 and 1,300 Lebanese and 165 Israelis (121 soldiers and 44 civilians) died, according to estimates: 1,191 is the figure of the Lebanese Higher Relief Council, and Human Rights Watch estimated that most of the Lebanese dead were civilians. Hezbollah admitted to 250 fighters killed, and Israel's foreign ministry spoke of more than 600. There were nearly a million Lebanese displaced and between 300,000 and 500,000 Israelis. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International accused both sides: Hezbollah of indiscriminate rockets, and Israel of attacks on civilian infrastructure and cluster bombs, especially in the last three days; the Winograd Commission rejected the claim that Israel committed war crimes. Security Council Resolution 1701 (11 August) called for the disarmament of Hezbollah and the deployment of the Lebanese army and UNIFIL; both sides claimed victory, and the Winograd Commission judged that Israel lost an opportunity by not achieving disarmament.

hechos/operacion-huerto/resumen.texto: Shortly after midnight on 6 September 2007, Israeli aircraft bombed a building under construction at Al Kibar, in the Syrian region of Deir ez-Zor. Israel and the United States did not announce it for seven months; the United States later said it was a nuclear facility for military purposes, and Syria denied this. The IAEA reported uranium and graphite in 2009, and in 2011 it concluded that the site was “most likely” a nuclear reactor that Syria should have declared; Syria did not cooperate with the investigation, and Israel acknowledged the attack only in 2018.

hechos/atentado-del-world-trade-center-1.texto: On 26 February 1993, Ramzi Yousef and his accomplices detonated a van carrying about 680 kg of explosives beneath the North Tower, intending to topple it onto the South Tower; six people were killed and more than a thousand were injured. In 1994 four men were sentenced to 240 years in prison, and in 1997 Yousef, the organizer, and Eyad Ismoil, the driver, were sentenced. According to journalist Steve Coll, shortly before the attack Yousef sent letters to New York newspapers signed “Liberation Army, Fifth Battalion,” demanding that the United States stop helping Israel, break relations with it and stop intervening in the Middle East. The FBI informant Emad Salem, in recordings, claimed that an FBI supervisor had discarded a plan to replace the explosive with a harmless powder; federal authorities denied this.

hechos/terremoto-de-beirut-551/resumen.texto: On 9 July 551, an earthquake of estimated magnitude 7.5 and a tsunami destroyed cities along the coast of Byzantine Phoenicia, from Tyre to Tripoli. The anonymous Pilgrim of Piacenza reports 30,000 dead in Berytus (Beirut) alone; Malalas and Agathias describe the destruction, and according to Agathias many young people who were studying law there died, and the professors of the famous law school moved to Sidon until Berytus was rebuilt. The emperor gave economic aid. The damage at Petra and in the Jordan Valley that was attributed to it is now more often explained by a later earthquake.

hechos/sitio-de-tripoli-1102/resumen.texto: Raymond of Toulouse, after taking Tortosa (1102), built the fortress Mons Peregrinus next to Tripoli to isolate it; he died in 1105 without seeing its fall. The city, whose Fatimid qadi Fajr al-Mulk ibn Ammar governed from 1099 to 1109, resisted until the Crusaders (Baldwin I of Jerusalem, Tancred and Bertrand of Toulouse, son of Raymond, with Genoese, Pisan and Provençal troops) took it on 12 July: they sacked it, enslaved many inhabitants and expelled the rest; the Egyptian fleet arrived eight hours late. Thus the County of Tripoli, the fourth Crusader state, was born.

hechos/caida-de-tripoli-1289/resumen.texto: The Mamluk sultan Qalawun besieged the Crusader county of Tripoli from March 1289 and took the city on 26 April, ending 180 years of uninterrupted Christian rule, the longest of the Frankish conquests in the Levant. The population was killed, although many escaped by sea; refugees from the island of Saint Thomas were captured on 29 April. Qalawun razed the city and ordered a new one built a few kilometers inland.

hechos/senorio-de-transjordania/resumen.texto: One of the main lordships of the Crusader kingdom of Jerusalem, east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea as far as the Gulf of Aqaba. Baldwin I built the castle of Montreal (1115) and around 1118 gave it to Romanus of Le Puy; in 1142 Fulk raised the castle of Kerak, which became its capital. It lived off desert agriculture and the tolls on caravans. Its last lord, Reginald of Châtillon, harassed merchants and pilgrims bound for Mecca, which gave Saladin a pretext to invade the kingdom in 1187; Saladin executed him after Hattin, and by 1189 he occupied all of Transjordan.
