hechos/asentamiento-circasiano-de-aman/r.texto: Circassian refugees from the Caucasus, expelled after the Russian conquest in the 1860s (which Circassian communities and several countries call genocide, a characterization Russia rejects) and after the Russo-Turkish war of 1877–1878, were settled by the Ottoman government in Transjordan, in Amman and Jerash, to farm the land and check the Bedouin. In 1878 some 50,000 Circassians arrived by sea in the Levant; they are credited with refounding Amman, which had been abandoned.

hechos/campana-de-mahdia-1087/resumen.texto: Attack on Mahdia by ships from Genoa and Pisa, with Rome's support, against the capital of the Zirid Tamim ibn Muizz, whose corsairs attacked Italians. They took the city, burned its fleet and collected an indemnity, part of which Pisa used to pay for its cathedral. The historian Carl Erdmann considered it a direct precedent of the First Crusade, because it was carried out under the banner of Saint Peter; others argue that destroying the Mahdia fleet later made it easier to supply the Crusaders by sea.

hechos/octava-cruzada/resumen.texto: Second crusade of Louis IX of France, directed against the Hafsid caliphate of Tunis. There was almost no fighting: the king died of dysentery shortly after arriving, and on 1 November 1270 Philip III, Charles of Anjou and Theobald II of Navarre signed with the Hafsid al-Mustansir the Treaty of Tunis, without territorial changes: the Christians obtained freedom of trade and worship, Charles received a third of a war indemnity, and the Hafsid resumed the tribute he owed to the king of Sicily. The historian Saba Malaspina believed that Charles of Anjou persuaded his brother to attack Tunis in order to collect the tribute that Tunis had paid to the kings of Sicily; Louis never stopped thinking of liberating Jerusalem.

hechos/asedio-de-tripoli-1551/resumen.texto: In August 1551 the Ottomans, with Sinan Pasha and the corsair Dragut, took Tripoli, held by the Knights Hospitaller since 1530, when Spain gave it to them along with Malta; the governor surrendered after six days of bombardment. It was, apparently, a reprisal for the Spanish and Hospitaller capture of Mahdia the previous year, which followed a raid on Gozo in which 5,000 to 7,000 inhabitants were enslaved. Through the intervention of the French ambassador, the knights and part of the garrison were allowed to leave for Malta, and the rest were killed or enslaved; Dragut made Tripoli a base for the Barbary corsairs.

hechos/batalla-de-chaldiran/resumen.texto: On 23 August 1514 Sultan Selim I defeated the Safavid shah Ismail I, who was wounded and nearly captured, with an Ottoman army of 60,000 to 100,000 men and much artillery, against 40,000 to 80,000 Safavids without artillery. The Ottomans annexed eastern Anatolia and northern Mesopotamia, occupied Tabriz and plundered its treasury, and the Kurdish chiefs passed from the Safavids to the Ottomans. It began 41 years of war, until the Peace of Amasya (1555); the Safavids recovered the region under Abbas I, but ceded it for good in the Treaty of Zuhab (1639).

hechos/rebeliones-celalies/resumen.texto: Rebellions of irregular troops led by band leaders and provincial officials (Celalis) against the Ottoman Empire in Anatolia, from the late 16th century until the mid-17th. The name comes from Bozoklu Celal, who rebelled in 1519; later rebellions, unrelated to his, were given his name. According to Mustafa Akdağ's periodization, they had a phase from 1596 to 1603 and another from 1604 to 1610. The Armenian bishop Grigor Daranaghtsi, himself a refugee, attributed them to Mehmed III's abandonment of Anatolia, corruption, the confiscation of land and famine; there were famines, abandoned villages and refugees, among them many Armenians who settled in Smyrna. Kuyucu Murad Pasha, nicknamed “the pit-digger” for the mass graves, suppressed them in 1606–1608.

hechos/sumision-del-hiyaz-1517/titulo.texto: The sharifs of Mecca recognize the Ottomans

hechos/sumision-del-hiyaz-1517/resumen.texto: After the Ottoman conquest of Egypt (1517), the sharif of Mecca, Barakat, recognized the supremacy of Sultan Selim I and sent him his son Abu Numayy with the keys of the holy cities and gifts; the sultan confirmed him and his son as joint rulers of the Hijaz. The sharifs retained much autonomy and, together with the Ottomans, extended their authority as far as Medina and Asir.

hechos/conflictos-otomano-portugueses/re.texto: After dominating the Red Sea from 1517, the Ottoman Empire and Portugal, which controlled the Indian Ocean from Goa, contested the routes of the Indian Ocean, the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea. In 1538 the fleet of Hadim Suleiman Pasha unsuccessfully besieged Diu, in India, and on the way back conquered almost all of Yemen, including Aden, which rebelled in 1548 and was retaken. In 1551 the Portuguese and their vassals from Hormuz took the fort of Qatif, which the Ottomans had occupied.

hechos/guerra-otomano-safavida-1532/resu.texto: War between Suleiman I and Shah Tahmasp I, sparked by territorial disputes, the switch of the bey of Bitlis to the Persian side, and Tahmasp's murder of the governor of Baghdad, who was sympathetic to Suleiman. Grand Vizier Ibrahim Pasha took Tabriz (July 1534), and Suleiman took Baghdad (December 1534), which had been in Safavid hands since 1508. Tahmasp avoided decisive battles and harassed the Ottomans. The Peace of Amasya (1555) confirmed the Ottoman gains.

hechos/toma-de-bagdad-1638/resumen.texto: Abbas I had taken Baghdad from the Ottomans in 1624, and several attempts to recover it failed. In 1638 Sultan Murad IV personally led the siege (from 15 November), with an army which a witness, Zarain Agha, estimated at 108,589 men; the Safavids had multiplied the garrison four- or fivefold. The city fell on 25 December, and the Treaty of Zuhab (17 May 1639) fixed the border with Persia.

lugares/cupula-de-la-roca/resumen.texto: Octagonal shrine built by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik in 691–692 over the rock of the Temple Mount, where Jewish tradition places the sacrifice of Isaac and Islamic tradition the Night Journey of Muhammad. It is the oldest surviving monumental Islamic building; the crusaders used it as a church, the Templum Domini.

lugares/mezquita-al-aqsa/resumen.texto: The “farthest mosque” of the Quran, at the southern end of the Temple Mount esplanade, the third holiest site in Islam. The crusaders turned it into a royal palace and later the headquarters of the Templars, who took their name from it.

lugares/santo-sepulcro/resumen.texto: Built by order of Constantine over the site that tradition identifies with Calvary and the tomb of Jesus. It was destroyed by the Persians in 614 and by the caliph al-Hakim in 1009; its rebuilding and custody were a central cause of the crusades. Today it is shared by six Churches under the Ottoman status quo.

lugares/muro-occidental/resumen.texto: A section of the retaining wall that Herod built around the Temple Mount. Since the Middle Ages it has been the great Jewish place of prayer; Muslims call it the al-Buraq Wall, and the 1929 riots began with a dispute over its use.

lugares/iglesia-de-la-natividad/resumen.texto: Basilica in Bethlehem built by Constantine and Helena over the grotto where tradition places the birth of Jesus, and rebuilt by Justinian. According to one tradition, the Persians spared it in 614 because the mosaic of the Magi showed them in Persian dress.

lugares/cueva-de-los-patriarcas/resumen.texto: The Herodian enclosure in Hebron over the Cave of Machpelah, where tradition places the tombs of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their wives. Sacred to Jews and Muslims, it was a mosque for centuries; the 1994 massacre took place there.

lugares/mar-saba/resumen.texto: Monastery in the Judaean Desert founded by Saint Sabbas. John of Damascus, the first great Christian theologian to write about Islam from within the caliphate, lived and wrote there.

lugares/belen/resumen.texto: City of David according to the Bible and birthplace of Jesus according to the Gospels. Saint Jerome lived there for 34 years and translated the Bible into Latin, the Vulgate.

lugares/nazaret/resumen.texto: Village in Galilee where Jesus grew up. Today it is the largest Arab city in Israel.

lugares/hebron/resumen.texto: One of the oldest cities of Canaan, David's first capital and site of the tomb of the patriarchs. It had an almost continuous Jewish community until the 1929 massacre.

lugares/jerico/resumen.texto: One of the oldest permanent settlements in the world, with a Neolithic tower and wall. According to the Book of Joshua, its walls fell before the Israelites.

lugares/cesarea-maritima/resumen.texto: Port built by Herod in honor of Augustus, later capital of the Roman province. Origen taught and Eusebius wrote there, and its library was the largest in Christian Palestine; Baibars razed it in 1265.

lugares/acre/resumen.texto: Main port of the crusaders and, between 1191 and 1291, capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Its fall to the Mamluks in 1291 ended the Crusader States; Napoleon failed before its walls in 1799.

lugares/jaffa/resumen.texto: Ancient port of Jerusalem, through which pilgrims arrived. Tel Aviv grew out of its outskirts in 1909.

lugares/tel-aviv/resumen.texto: First modern Hebrew city, founded next to Jaffa. There Ben-Gurion declared the independence of Israel on 14 May 1948.

lugares/haifa/resumen.texto: Port on Mount Carmel, industrial center of the Mandate and world center of the Bahá'í Faith.

lugares/gaza/resumen.texto: Philistine city, incense port, center of late Greek rhetoric and, according to tradition, site of the tomb of Muhammad's great-grandfather. Sabbatai Zevi proclaimed himself messiah there in 1665. Capital of the Gaza Strip, governed by Hamas since 2007.

lugares/ascalon/resumen.texto: Philistine city and great Fatimid fortress, the last on the coast to fall to the crusaders (1153). Baibars destroyed it in 1270.

lugares/tiberias/resumen.texto: Founded by Herod Antipas on the Sea of Galilee. It was the seat of the patriarchate and of the Jewish academies where the Mishnah, the Jerusalem Talmud and the Masoretic vocalization of the Bible were fixed; the tomb of Maimonides is there.

lugares/safed/resumen.texto: City in the mountains of Galilee where kabbalists expelled from Spain gathered in the 16th century: Joseph Caro, Moses Cordovero and Isaac Luria. It is one of the four holy cities of Judaism.

lugares/meguido/resumen.texto: Fortified city that controlled the pass from the coast to the Jezreel Valley, the scene of battles since Thutmose III. Its Greek name, Armageddon, is the site of the final battle in the Book of Revelation.

lugares/laquis/resumen.texto: Second city of Judah. Its siege by Sennacherib in 701 BC was recorded in the reliefs of Nineveh, and its letters in Hebrew describe the last days before the Babylonian conquest.

lugares/qumran/resumen.texto: Settlement by the Dead Sea, near the caves where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found from 1947 onward. Many scholars attribute it to an Essene community; it was destroyed by the Romans c. 68.

lugares/masada/resumen.texto: Herod's palace-fortress on a plateau in the Judaean Desert. According to Josephus, its last Jewish defenders took their own lives before the Romans captured it in 73 or 74.

lugares/samaria/resumen.texto: Capital of the Kingdom of Israel from King Omri until its conquest by Assyria in 722 BC. Herod rebuilt it as Sebaste.

lugares/nablus/resumen.texto: Flavia Neapolis, founded by Vespasian next to ancient Shechem. Center of the Samaritans, who revere nearby Mount Gerizim.

lugares/monte-gerizim/resumen.texto: The sacred mountain of the Samaritans, where they had their temple until John Hyrcanus destroyed it c. 110 BC. They still celebrate Passover there.

lugares/cafarnaum/resumen.texto: Fishing village on the Sea of Galilee where, according to the Gospels, Jesus lived and preached. A synagogue from the 4th or 5th century survives, along with a church over what is believed to be Peter's house.

lugares/seforis/resumen.texto: Capital of Galilee, where Judah ha-Nasi completed the redaction of the Mishnah c. 200. It preserves Roman mosaics and a synagogue with a zodiac.

lugares/hazor/resumen.texto: The largest Canaanite city, “the head of all those kingdoms” according to the Book of Joshua, destroyed c. 13th century BC.

lugares/beerseba/resumen.texto: City in the Negev associated in the Bible with Abraham. The British took it in 1917 with a famous Australian cavalry charge.

lugares/ramla/resumen.texto: The only city in Palestine founded by the Arabs, capital of the province of Filastin from the caliph Sulayman onward. It was the region's principal city until the Crusades.

lugares/atlit/resumen.texto: Templar fortress on the coast, never taken by assault; it was evacuated after the fall of Acre.

lugares/universidad-hebrea/resumen.texto: Its foundation stone was laid in 1918 and it opened in 1925. Its founders and professors included Einstein, Martin Buber and Gershom Scholem, who made Kabbalah a subject of academic study.

lugares/universidad-de-birzeit/resumen.texto: Founded as a school in 1924 and a university since 1975, near Ramallah; one of the centers of Palestinian intellectual life.

lugares/beirut/resumen.texto: Phoenician port and seat of the great school of Roman law until the earthquake of 551. From the 19th century it was the center of the Arab cultural revival (the Nahda) and of the missionary universities.

lugares/sidon/resumen.texto: One of the great Phoenician cities; it was a Crusader lordship and retains a 13th-century Sea Castle.

lugares/tripoli-libano/resumen.texto: Capital of the Crusader County of Tripoli from 1109 until its capture by the Mamluks in 1289. Before the Crusader conquest it had a famous library, the House of Knowledge of the Banu Ammar.

lugares/baalbek/resumen.texto: The Roman Heliopolis in the Beqaa Valley, with the temples of Jupiter and Bacchus, among the largest in the Roman world.

lugares/damasco/resumen.texto: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, an Aramaean capital and later capital of the Umayyad Caliphate. It was the great center of the jihad against the Crusaders under Nur al-Din and Saladin, who is buried beside its great mosque.

lugares/mezquita-de-los-omeyas/resumen.texto: Built by the caliph al-Walid I on the site of the Cathedral of Saint John the Baptist, which had earlier been a temple of Jupiter. Its landscape mosaics are the work of Byzantine craftsmen.

lugares/alepo/resumen.texto: Great commercial city of northern Syria and court of the Hamdanid emir Sayf al-Dawla, patron of al-Farabi and the poet al-Mutanabbi. It resisted the Crusaders and was besieged by them in 1124.

lugares/antioquia/resumen.texto: Seleucid capital and one of the great cities of the Roman Empire, where the followers of Jesus were first called Christians. The Crusaders took it in 1098 after a long siege, and it was the capital of a principality until 1268.

lugares/palmira/resumen.texto: Caravan city in the Syrian Desert whose queen Zenobia defied Rome in the 3rd century. The Islamic State destroyed some of its temples in 2015.

lugares/krak-de-los-caballeros/resumen.texto: The fortress of the Hospitallers, the best-preserved Crusader castle; Baibars took it in 1271.

lugares/hama/resumen.texto: City on the Orontes known for its norias. Its Ayyubid emir Abu'l-Fida, who fought in the capture of Acre, wrote a universal history and a geography.

lugares/masyaf/resumen.texto: Main castle of the Nizari Ismailis of Syria, the “Assassins”, ruled in the 12th century by Rashid al-Din Sinan, the “Old Man of the Mountain”.

lugares/aman/resumen.texto: The biblical Rabbath Ammon and the Philadelphia of the Decapolis; capital of the Emirate of Transjordan from 1921.

lugares/petra/resumen.texto: Capital of the Nabataeans, carved into rose-colored rock, which lived off the incense trade. Trajan annexed it in 106.

lugares/jerash/resumen.texto: The Gerasa of the Decapolis, one of the best-preserved Roman cities in the East.

lugares/madaba/resumen.texto: Moabite and later Byzantine city, famous for the 6th-century mosaic map of the Holy Land preserved in its Church of Saint George.

lugares/monte-nebo/resumen.texto: According to Deuteronomy, from here Moses saw the Promised Land before he died. It has a Byzantine sanctuary with mosaics.

lugares/kerak/resumen.texto: Crusader castle that dominated the caravan route between Damascus and Mecca; from there Raynald of Châtillon attacked Muslim pilgrims, and Saladin took it in 1188.

lugares/la-meca/resumen.texto: City of the Quraysh tribe, birthplace of Muhammad and site of the Kaaba. It is the destination of the pilgrimage (hajj) and the direction Muslims face in prayer; it is closed to non-Muslims.

lugares/kaaba/resumen.texto: The cube-shaped sanctuary at the center of Mecca, filled with idols before Islam. Muhammad purified it in 630 and dedicated it to the one God; the Quran attributes it to Abraham and Ishmael.

lugares/medina/resumen.texto: Ancient Yathrib, an oasis inhabited by Arab and Jewish tribes. Muhammad emigrated there in 622, and the city was the capital of the first Islamic state until 656.

lugares/mezquita-del-profeta/resumen.texto: Built by Muhammad next to his house when he arrived in Medina; his tomb is there.

lugares/taif/resumen.texto: Mountain city of the Thaqif tribe, which rejected Muhammad in 619 and surrendered to him in 630.

lugares/jaibar/resumen.texto: Oasis of Jewish tribes north of Medina, conquered by Muhammad in 628; its inhabitants were allowed to stay as sharecroppers until Umar expelled them.

lugares/sana/resumen.texto: Capital of Yemen since antiquity, with its Great Mosque, where one of the oldest Quran manuscripts was found in 1972.

lugares/cartago/resumen.texto: Phoenician colony that became the leading power of the western Mediterranean, destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and refounded as the capital of Roman Africa. It was the city of Tertullian, Cyprian and the young Augustine; the Arabs took it in 698.

lugares/cairuan/resumen.texto: Founded by Uqba ibn Nafi as a camp and base for the conquest of the Maghreb; it was the capital of the Aghlabids and a great center of Maliki law.

lugares/gran-mezquita-de-cairuan/resumen.texto: Founded together with the city and rebuilt by the Aghlabids in the 9th century; its minaret is one of the oldest in Islam.

lugares/tunez/resumen.texto: Capital of the Hafsids from the 13th century. Louis IX died there during his second crusade (1270), and Ibn Khaldun was born there (1332).

lugares/fez/resumen.texto: Founded by the Idrisids, it took in refugees from Kairouan and Córdoba. It was the capital of the Marinids and the great intellectual center of the Maghreb.

lugares/al-qarawiyyin/resumen.texto: Mosque and school in Fez founded by Fatima al-Fihri, a woman from Kairouan; it is often cited as one of the oldest educational institutions still in operation.

lugares/argel/resumen.texto: City refounded in the 10th century; from 1516 the capital of the Ottoman regency and its corsairs, against which Charles V failed in 1541. France conquered it in 1830.

lugares/tripoli-libia/resumen.texto: The Phoenician Oea; taken by the Arabs in 643, by Spain in 1510 and by the Ottomans in 1551.

lugares/tremecen/resumen.texto: Capital of the Zayyanids between the 13th and 16th centuries.

lugares/mahdia/resumen.texto: Capital founded by the first Fatimid caliph, from which his dynasty prepared the conquest of Egypt.

lugares/cirene/resumen.texto: Greek colony of Thera, birthplace of Aristippus and Eratosthenes, with a large Jewish community that rebelled against Rome in 115.

lugares/nicosia/resumen.texto: Capital of the Lusignan kings, who were crowned in its Cathedral of Saint Sophia, converted into a mosque in 1570.

lugares/famagusta/resumen.texto: Port where the Christians of Syria took refuge after 1291 and where the kings of Cyprus were crowned kings of Jerusalem. It held out against the Ottomans for almost a year before surrendering in 1571.

lugares/limasol/resumen.texto: Richard the Lionheart landed there in 1191 and married Berengaria of Navarre.

lugares/bagdad/resumen.texto: Capital founded by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur. With the House of Wisdom and the translations from Greek, it was the center of learning of the Islamic world until the Mongols sacked it in 1258.
